questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of leaf features to distinguish a dorsiventral (dicot) leaf from an isobilateral (monocot) leaf and explaining the role of bulliform cells
questions.question:
A student records features of two leaf sections.

Feature | Leaf P | Leaf Q
Mesophyll | palisade (adaxial) and spongy (abaxial) | not differentiated
Stomata | more on the abaxial (lower) epidermis | about equal on both surfaces
Venation | reticulate, veins of varying size | parallel, veins of similar size
Special epidermal cells | absent | large, empty, colourless cells on the adaxial side

Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) P is isobilateral (monocot) and Q dorsiventral (dicot)
B) Both are dicot leaves differing only in age

C) P is a dorsiventral dicot leaf and Q an isobilateral monocot leaf; the large colourless adaxial cells of Q are bulliform cells, which become flaccid when they lose water so that the leaf curls inwards to reduce water loss; in both leaves the vascular bundles are surrounded by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells
D) The special cells in Q are guard cells that open stomata at night
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P dorsiventral dicot, Q isobilateral monocot; bulliform cells allow leaf rolling; bundle sheath around vascular bundles.
Concept: The vertical section of a dorsiventral leaf through the lamina shows three main parts: epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system. The epidermis which covers both the upper surface (adaxial epidermis) and lower surface (abaxial epidermis) of the leaf has a conspicuous cuticle; the abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata than the adaxial epidermis, and the latter may even lack stomata. The mesophyll, which possesses chloroplasts and carries out photosynthesis, is made up of parenchyma and has two types of cells — the palisade parenchyma (elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other, adaxially placed) and the spongy parenchyma (oval or round, loosely arranged cells situated below the palisade cells and extending to the lower epidermis). Vascular bundles can be seen in the veins and the midrib; the size of the vascular bundles is dependent on the size of the veins, which vary in thickness in the reticulate venation of dicot leaves; the vascular bundles are surrounded by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells. The anatomy of an isobilateral (monocot) leaf is similar to that of the dorsiventral leaf in many ways, with the following characteristic differences: the stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis, and the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma. In grasses, certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins modify themselves into large, empty, colourless cells called bulliform cells; when the bulliform cells in the leaves have absorbed water and are turgid, the leaf surface is exposed; when they are flaccid due to water stress, they make the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss. The parallel venation in monocot leaves is reflected in the near similar sizes of vascular bundles (except in main veins).
Given: Four features of leaves P and Q.
Step 1: Palisade/spongy differentiation and more abaxial stomata ⇒ P dorsiventral.
Step 2: Undifferentiated mesophyll, stomata on both surfaces, parallel veins ⇒ Q isobilateral.
Step 3: Large empty adaxial cells ⇒ bulliform cells.
Why: Leaf anatomy reflects light exposure and water economy: a horizontally held dicot leaf has distinct upper and lower tissues, while a vertically held grass leaf has both surfaces alike.
Why not the others: (A) Labels reversed. (B) The differences are structural, not due to age. (D) Bulliform cells are not guard cells.
Key point: Dorsiventral: palisade + spongy, more abaxial stomata; isobilateral: uniform mesophyll, bulliform cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of packaging of DNA from the double helix to the metaphase chromosome, and the structure of the nucleus and the classification of chromosomes by centromere position
questions.question: Which sequence and description of nuclear organisation is correct?
options: A) Negatively charged DNA wraps around a positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome (about 200 bp of DNA) → repeating nucleosomes form a 'beads-on-string' chromatin fibre → the fibre is further coiled and supercoiled into chromatin fibres, which condense into chromosomes at metaphase, a process requiring non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins; the nucleus is bounded by two membranes with a perinuclear space and nuclear pores, and chromosomes are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric depending on the position of the centromere
B) Histones wrap around DNA, forming chromosomes directly, and the nuclear envelope is a single membrane
C) Nucleosomes form after chromosomes condense at metaphase
D) A telocentric chromosome has its centromere exactly in the middle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) DNA + histone octamer → nucleosome → beads-on-string → chromatin fibres → metaphase chromosome; double nuclear envelope; four centromere types.
Concept: The distance between two consecutive base pairs is 0.34 nm, so the length of DNA in a typical mammalian cell (6.6 × 10⁹ bp) is about 2.2 metres — far greater than the dimension of a typical nucleus (approximately 10⁻⁶ m). In eukaryotes, there is a set of positively charged, basic proteins called histones, rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine, which carry positive charges in their side chains; histones are organised to form a unit of eight molecules called a histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around the positively charged histone octamer to form a structure called the nucleosome; a typical nucleosome contains 200 bp of DNA helix. Nucleosomes constitute the repeating unit of a structure in the nucleus called chromatin, thread-like stained (coloured) bodies seen in the nucleus; the nucleosomes in chromatin are seen as 'beads-on-string' under the electron microscope. The beads-on-string structure in chromatin is packaged to form chromatin fibres that are further coiled and condensed at the metaphase stage of cell division to form chromosomes; the packaging of chromatin at a higher level requires an additional set of proteins collectively referred to as non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins. The nuclear envelope, which consists of two parallel membranes with a space between (10 to 50 nm) called the perinuclear space, forms a barrier between the materials present inside the nucleus and those of the cytoplasm; the outer membrane usually remains continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum; at a number of places the nuclear envelope is interrupted by minute pores. Every chromosome essentially has a primary constriction, the centromere; based on its position, chromosomes are metacentric (middle centromere, two equal arms), sub-metacentric (centromere slightly away from the middle, one shorter and one longer arm), acrocentric (centromere situated close to its end, one extremely short and one very long arm) and telocentric (terminal centromere).
Step 1: DNA wraps the histone octamer ⇒ nucleosome.
Step 2: Nucleosomes in series ⇒ beads-on-string chromatin.
Step 3: Further coiling with NHC proteins ⇒ chromatin fibres ⇒ metaphase chromosomes.
Why: Opposite charges on DNA and histones allow the very long DNA to be packed in stages into the small nucleus.
Why not the others: (B) DNA wraps histones; the envelope is double. (C) Order reversed. (D) Telocentric means terminal centromere.
Key point: DNA → nucleosome (200 bp) → beads-on-string → chromatin fibre → chromosome.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting rate measurements of an enzyme at different substrate concentrations, with an inhibitor, and after exposure to low and high temperatures
questions.question: An enzyme's reaction rate is measured. (i) Rate rises with substrate concentration and levels off at a maximum. (ii) With substance X present, a higher substrate concentration is needed to reach half the maximum rate, but the same maximum is reached at very high substrate concentration. (iii) Enzyme kept at 4 °C is inactive, but regains activity when warmed to 37 °C. (iv) Enzyme heated to 70 °C stays inactive after cooling. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (ii) X is a non-competitive inhibitor that destroys the active site
B) (iii) and (iv) both show permanent denaturation
C) (i) shows that the rate increases indefinitely with substrate

D) (i) At high substrate concentration all active sites are occupied, so the rate approaches Vmax; (ii) X is a competitive inhibitor resembling the substrate, raising Km but not Vmax, because excess substrate outcompetes it; (iii) low temperature only temporarily inactivates the enzyme; (iv) high temperature denatures the protein and destroys its active site permanently
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Saturation gives Vmax; X competitive (Km ↑, Vmax unchanged); cold reversibly inactivates; heat denatures.
Concept: The activity of an enzyme can be affected by a change in the conditions which can alter the tertiary structure of the protein; these include temperature, pH, change in substrate concentration or binding of specific chemicals that regulate its activity. Enzymes generally function in a narrow range of temperature and pH; each enzyme shows its highest activity at a particular temperature and pH called the optimum temperature and optimum pH; activity declines both below and above the optimum value; low temperature preserves the enzyme in a temporarily inactive state whereas high temperature destroys enzymatic activity because proteins are denatured by heat. With the increase in substrate concentration, the velocity of the enzymatic reaction rises at first; the reaction ultimately reaches a maximum velocity (Vmax) which is not exceeded by any further rise in concentration of the substrate; this is because the enzyme molecules are fewer than the substrate molecules and after saturation of these molecules, there are no free enzyme molecules to bind with the additional substrate molecules. When the inhibitor closely resembles the substrate in its molecular structure and inhibits the activity of the enzyme, it is known as a competitive inhibitor; because it competes with the substrate for the active site, its effect is overcome by raising substrate concentration, so the substrate concentration needed for half-maximal rate (Km) rises while Vmax stays the same.
Step 1: Levelling off ⇒ saturation at Vmax.
Step 2: Same Vmax, higher substrate for half Vmax ⇒ competitive inhibition.
Step 3: 4 °C reversible; 70 °C irreversible denaturation.
Why: Enzyme activity depends on substrate access to an intact active site; competition can be outweighed, but a heat-denatured site cannot recover.
Why not the others: (A) A competitive inhibitor does not lower Vmax. (B) Cold inactivation is reversible. (C) The rate saturates.
Key point: Vmax at saturation; competitive inhibitor raises Km only; cold reversible, heat irreversible.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effect of a spindle-inhibiting drug and of failed cytokinesis on mitosis, chromosome number and cell structure, and the significance of mitosis
questions.question: Onion root tips (2n = 16) are treated with colchicine, which prevents spindle formation. In another case, nuclear division occurs repeatedly without cytokinesis. Which prediction is correct?
options: A) Colchicine-treated cells complete anaphase normally, and the second case produces many separate cells

B) In colchicine-treated cells chromosomes cannot separate, so cells accumulate with condensed chromosomes as in metaphase, and if the cell enters interphase it becomes polyploid (32 chromosomes); repeated karyokinesis without cytokinesis gives a multinucleate condition (syncytium), as in the liquid endosperm of coconut; normally mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant, restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, and helps growth, repair and the replacement of cells such as those of the gut lining and blood
C) Colchicine reduces the chromosome number to 8
D) Mitosis occurs only in haploid cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Arrest with condensed chromosomes, polyploidy (32); syncytium without cytokinesis; significance of mitosis.
Concept: Mitosis or the equational division is usually restricted to the diploid cells only; however, in some lower plants and in some social insects haploid cells also divide by mitosis. In metaphase, spindle fibres attach to kinetochores of chromosomes, and chromosomes align at the metaphase plate; in anaphase, centromeres split and chromatids separate and move to opposite poles; this movement requires the spindle. Thus a drug that prevents spindle formation stops chromosome movement, so cells remain with condensed, metaphase-like chromosomes; if such a cell re-forms a nucleus without dividing, its chromosome number is doubled. Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm; in some organisms karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, as a result of which a multinucleate condition arises leading to the formation of a syncytium (e.g. liquid endosperm in coconut). Mitosis results in the production of diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement usually; the growth of multicellular organisms is due to mitosis; cell growth results in disturbing the ratio between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, so it becomes essential for the cell to divide to restore the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio; a very significant contribution of mitosis is cell repair — the cells of the upper layer of the epidermis, cells of the lining of the gut and blood cells are being constantly replaced; mitotic divisions in the meristematic tissues result in a continuous growth of plants throughout their life.
Step 1: No spindle ⇒ no anaphase ⇒ metaphase-like arrest.
Step 2: Re-formed nucleus has both sets ⇒ 2 × 16 = 32 chromosomes.
Step 3: Karyokinesis without cytokinesis ⇒ syncytium.
Why: Chromatid separation needs spindle fibres, and cell separation needs cytokinesis; blocking either changes the outcome predictably.
Why not the others: (A) Anaphase needs the spindle; nuclei stay in one cell. (C) Chromosome number doubles, not halves. (D) Mitosis occurs mainly in diploid cells.
Key point: Colchicine blocks spindle ⇒ polyploidy; no cytokinesis ⇒ syncytium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of events in non-cyclic photophosphorylation from light absorption to NADPH formation, the site of water splitting, and the difference from cyclic photophosphorylation
questions.question: Which sequence and description of the light reaction is correct?
options: A) Light excites the reaction centre P680 of PS II, and its electron is accepted by a primary acceptor → the electron passes down an electron transport chain of cytochromes to P700 of PS I → P700, also excited by light, passes electrons through another chain to NADP⁺, reducing it to NADPH + H⁺ (the Z scheme); electrons lost by PS II are replaced by splitting water on the inner (lumen) side of the thylakoid, releasing O₂ and H⁺; protons accumulate in the lumen and flow out through the CF₀ channel of ATP synthase, whose CF₁ part makes ATP; in cyclic photophosphorylation only PS I works, in the stroma lamellae, and only ATP is made
B) PS I acts first and passes electrons to PS II, which reduces NADP⁺
C) Water is split on the stromal side of the thylakoid, and O₂ is released by PS I
D) Cyclic photophosphorylation produces NADPH and O₂ but no ATP
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) PS II (P680) → ETC → PS I (P700) → NADPH; water split in lumen; ATP synthase CF₀/CF₁; cyclic = PS I only, ATP only.
Concept: The light reactions or the 'photochemical' phase include light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release, and the formation of high-energy chemical intermediates, ATP and NADPH. In photosystem II the reaction centre chlorophyll a absorbs 680 nm wavelength of red light, causing electrons to become excited and jump into an orbit farther from the atomic nucleus; these electrons are picked up by an electron acceptor which passes them to an electron transport system consisting of cytochromes; this movement of electrons is downhill in terms of an oxidation-reduction or redox potential scale; the electrons are not used up as they pass through the electron transport chain, but are passed on to the pigments of photosystem PS I. Simultaneously, electrons in the reaction centre of PS I are also excited when they receive red light of wavelength 700 nm and are transferred to another acceptor molecule that has a greater redox potential; these electrons then are moved downhill again, this time to a molecule of energy-rich NADP⁺; the addition of these electrons reduces NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺; this whole scheme of transfer of electrons, starting from the PS II, uphill to the acceptor, down the electron transport chain to PS I, excitation of electrons, transfer to another acceptor, and finally down hill to NADP⁺ causing it to be reduced to NADPH + H⁺ is called the Z scheme. The electrons that were moved from photosystem II must be replaced; this is achieved by electrons available due to splitting of water; the water splitting complex is associated with the PS II, which itself is physically located on the inner side of the membrane of the thylakoid; water is split into H⁺, [O] and electrons. The proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is broken down due to the movement of protons across the membrane to the stroma through the transmembrane channel of the CF₀ of the ATP synthase; the CF₁ portion undergoes conformational changes allowing ATP synthesis. When only PS I is functional, the electron is circulated within the photosystem and the phosphorylation occurs due to cyclic flow of electrons; a possible location where this could be happening is in the stroma lamellae, which lack PS II as well as NADP reductase enzyme; this results only in the synthesis of ATP, but not of NADPH + H⁺.
Step 1: PS II excited ⇒ electrons to primary acceptor ⇒ cytochrome chain.
Step 2: PS I excited ⇒ electrons to NADP⁺ ⇒ NADPH.
Step 3: Water split at PS II (lumen side) replaces electrons; proton gradient drives ATP synthase.
Why: Two light-driven boosts are needed to raise electrons from water to NADP⁺; the proton gradient formed along the way powers ATP synthesis.
Why not the others: (B) PS II acts first. (C) Water splitting is on the lumen side at PS II. (D) Cyclic flow makes ATP only.
Key point: Z scheme: H₂O → PS II → ETC → PS I → NADP⁺; ATP via chemiosmosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of intermediates and the steps that release CO₂ and reduce NAD⁺ and FAD in the Krebs (TCA) cycle, and the yield per pyruvate including the link reaction
questions.question: Which sequence and description of the TCA cycle is correct?
options: A) Citrate → oxaloacetate → acetyl CoA, with CO₂ released at every step
B) The cycle occurs in the cytoplasm and produces glucose

C) Acetyl CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) and water to form citrate (6C), catalysed by citrate synthase → citrate isomerises to isocitrate → two successive decarboxylations give α-ketoglutaric acid (5C) and then succinyl CoA (4C), each reducing NAD⁺ → succinyl CoA forms succinic acid with substrate-level phosphorylation of GDP to GTP → succinate is oxidised to fumarate (FAD reduced) → malate → oxaloacetate (NAD⁺ reduced); per pyruvate, including the link reaction, there are 3 CO₂, 4 NADH + H⁺, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP (ATP), all in the mitochondrial matrix
D) FAD is reduced during the conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Acetyl CoA + OAA → citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate → succinyl CoA → succinate (GTP) → fumarate (FADH₂) → malate → OAA (NADH); per pyruvate 3 CO₂, 4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP.
Concept: Pyruvate, which is formed by the glycolytic catabolism of carbohydrates in the cytosol, after it enters the mitochondrial matrix undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by a complex set of reactions catalysed by pyruvic dehydrogenase; the reactions require the participation of several coenzymes, including NAD⁺ and coenzyme A: pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺. The acetyl CoA then enters a cyclic pathway, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, more commonly called the Krebs' cycle after the scientist Hans Krebs who first elucidated it. The TCA cycle starts with the condensation of the acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to yield citric acid; the reaction is catalysed by the enzyme citrate synthase and a molecule of CoA is released; citrate is then isomerised to isocitrate; it is followed by two successive steps of decarboxylation, leading to the formation of α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-CoA; in the remaining steps of the citric acid cycle, succinyl-CoA is oxidised to OAA, allowing the cycle to continue; during the conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinic acid a molecule of GTP is synthesised — this is a substrate level phosphorylation; in a coupled reaction GTP is converted to GDP with the simultaneous synthesis of ATP from ADP; also there are three points in the cycle where NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH + H⁺ and one point where FAD⁺ is reduced to FADH₂. The continued oxidation of acetyl CoA via the TCA cycle requires the continued replenishment of oxaloacetic acid, the first member of the cycle, and also regeneration of NAD⁺ and FAD⁺ from NADH and FADH₂ respectively.
Step 1: Link reaction: 1 CO₂, 1 NADH.
Step 2: Cycle: 2 CO₂ (isocitrate → α-KG → succinyl CoA), 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP.
Step 3: Total per pyruvate: 3 CO₂, 4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP.
Why: Each turn completely oxidises the two carbons of acetyl CoA to CO₂, storing the released energy mostly as reduced coenzymes for the electron transport system.
Why not the others: (A) Order wrong; only two cycle steps release CO₂. (B) The cycle is in the matrix and oxidises, not makes, carbohydrate. (D) FAD is reduced at succinate → fumarate.
Key point: Two decarboxylations, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP per turn; OAA regenerated.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of ionic events from the resting membrane potential through depolarisation and repolarisation during conduction of a nerve impulse
questions.question: Which sequence and description of nerve impulse generation is correct?
options: A) At rest the inside is positive; K⁺ enters to depolarise the membrane
B) The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 2 Na⁺ out and 3 K⁺ in, making the inside positive at rest
C) Repolarisation occurs because Na⁺ channels open wider

D) At rest the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, and the sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, so the outer surface is positive and the inner negative (polarised, resting potential) → a stimulus makes the membrane freely permeable to Na⁺ at that site, Na⁺ rushes in and the polarity reverses (depolarisation, action potential) → the local current depolarises the next site, so the impulse moves along → the rise in Na⁺ permeability is short-lived and is followed by a rise in K⁺ permeability, K⁺ diffuses out and the resting potential is restored (repolarisation)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Resting polarisation by pump and K⁺ permeability → Na⁺ influx (depolarisation) → propagation → K⁺ efflux (repolarisation).
Concept: Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are in a polarised state. Different types of ion channels are present on the neural membrane; these ion channels are selectively permeable to different ions; when a neuron is not conducting any impulse, i.e. resting, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to potassium ions (K⁺) and nearly impermeable to sodium ions (Na⁺); similarly, the membrane is impermeable to negatively charged proteins present in the axoplasm; consequently, the axoplasm inside the axon contains a high concentration of K⁺ and negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of Na⁺; in contrast, the fluid outside the axon contains a low concentration of K⁺, a high concentration of Na⁺, and thus forms a concentration gradient. These ionic gradients across the resting membrane are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium-potassium pump which transports 3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ into the cell; as a result, the outer surface of the axonal membrane possesses a positive charge while its inner surface becomes negatively charged and therefore is polarised; the electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is called the resting potential. When a stimulus is applied at a site on the polarised membrane, the membrane at the site becomes freely permeable to Na⁺; this leads to a rapid influx of Na⁺ followed by the reversal of the polarity at that site, i.e. the outer surface of the membrane becomes negatively charged and the inner side becomes positively charged; the polarity of the membrane at that site is thus reversed and hence depolarised; the electrical potential difference across the plasma membrane at that site is called the action potential, which is in fact termed a nerve impulse. At sites immediately ahead, the axon membrane has a positive charge on the outer surface and a negative charge on its inner surface; as a result, a current flows on the inner surface from the depolarised site to the next site, so the action potential is generated there; thus, the impulse (action potential) generated at one site is conducted along the length of the axon. The rise in the stimulus-induced permeability to Na⁺ is extremely short-lived; it is quickly followed by a rise in permeability to K⁺; within a fraction of a second, K⁺ diffuses outside the membrane and restores the resting potential of the membrane at the site of excitation, and the fibre becomes once more responsive to further stimulation.
Step 1: Resting: inside negative (pump 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in; K⁺ permeability).
Step 2: Stimulus: Na⁺ influx ⇒ depolarisation (action potential).
Step 3: K⁺ efflux ⇒ repolarisation; local currents propagate the impulse.
Why: Timed opening of Na⁺ and then K⁺ channels reverses and restores membrane polarity, and local currents trigger the same sequence in the next region.
Why not the others: (A) Inside is negative at rest; Na⁺ entry depolarises. (B) Pump ratio reversed. (C) Repolarisation is due to K⁺ efflux.
Key point: Rest (inside −) → Na⁺ in (depolarise) → K⁺ out (repolarise).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the phenotypes of children from marriages involving haemophilia and colour blindness, using X-linked recessive inheritance
questions.question: (i) A woman whose father had haemophilia but whose husband is normal plans a family. (ii) A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. Which prediction is correct?
options: A) In (i) all children will be haemophilic; in (ii) all sons will be colour-blind

B) In (i) the woman must be a carrier (XᴴXʰ), so each son has a 50 % chance of haemophilia and each daughter a 50 % chance of being a carrier, with no affected daughters; in (ii) all daughters will be carriers with normal vision and all sons will have normal vision, because a father passes his X only to daughters
C) In (i) daughters will be haemophilic and sons normal
D) In (ii) half the daughters will be colour-blind
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (i) Sons 50 % affected, daughters 50 % carriers; (ii) all daughters carriers, all sons normal.
Concept: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease which shows its transmission from an unaffected carrier female to some of the male progeny; in this disease, a single protein that is a part of the cascade of proteins involved in the clotting of blood is affected; due to this, in an affected individual a simple cut will result in non-stop bleeding; the heterozygous female (carrier) for haemophilia may transmit the disease to sons; the possibility of a female becoming a haemophilic is extremely rare because the mother of such a female has to be at least a carrier and the father should be haemophilic. Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in either the red or green cone of the eye, resulting in failure to discriminate between red and green colour; this defect is due to mutation in certain genes present in the X chromosome; it occurs in about 8 per cent of males and only about 0.4 per cent of females; this is because the genes that lead to red-green colour blindness are on the X chromosome; males have only one X chromosome and females have two; the son of a woman who carries the gene has a 50 per cent chance of being colour blind; the mother is not herself colour blind because the gene is recessive, which means that its effect is suppressed by her matching dominant normal gene; a daughter will not normally be colour blind unless her mother is a carrier and her father is colour blind.
Given: (i) XᴴXʰ (her father XʰY) × XᴴY; (ii) XᶜY × XX (homozygous normal).
Step 1: (i) Daughter of a haemophilic father always receives Xʰ ⇒ carrier.
Step 2: (i) XᴴXʰ × XᴴY ⇒ XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY, XʰY ⇒ ½ sons affected, ½ daughters carriers.
Step 3: (ii) Father's affected X goes to every daughter (carriers); sons get mother's normal X.
Why: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes and receive their X only from their mother, so they express recessive alleles directly and cannot inherit them from their father.
Why not the others: (A) Only some sons in (i) and no sons in (ii) are affected. (C) Pattern reversed. (D) Daughters in (ii) receive a normal X from the mother.
Key point: X-linked recessive: carrier mother → ½ sons affected; affected father → all daughters carriers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating probabilities of affected, carrier and normal children when both parents are carriers of sickle-cell anaemia, and the molecular basis of sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia
questions.question: Both parents are carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) of sickle-cell anaemia. What is the probability that (a) a child is affected, (b) two successive children are both affected, and (c) a phenotypically normal child is a carrier; and which statement is correct?
options: A) 1/2; 1/4; 1/2; the mutation changes valine to glutamic acid
B) 1/4; 1/2; 1/3; thalassemia is a qualitative defect in globin

C) 1/4; 1/16; 2/3; sickle-cell anaemia is caused by substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) by valine (Val) at the sixth position of the β-globin chain (GAG → GUG), so the haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen and the RBCs become sickle-shaped, while thalassemia is a quantitative problem in which too few globin molecules are synthesised
D) 1/4; 1/8; 1/2; both disorders are X-linked
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/4; 1/16; 2/3; Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin; thalassemia is quantitative.
Concept: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are carriers for the gene (or heterozygous); the disease is controlled by a single pair of alleles, HbA and HbS; out of the three possible genotypes, only homozygous individuals for HbS (HbS HbS) show the diseased phenotype; heterozygous (HbA HbS) individuals appear apparently unaffected but they are carriers of the disease, as there is a 50 per cent probability of transmission of the mutant gene to the progeny, thus exhibiting sickle-cell trait. The defect is caused by the substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) by valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of the haemoglobin molecule; the substitution of amino acid in the globin protein results due to the single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene from GAG to GUG; the mutant haemoglobin molecule undergoes polymerisation under low oxygen tension, causing the change in the shape of the RBC from biconcave disc to elongated sickle-like structure. Thalassemia is also an autosome-linked recessive blood disease transmitted from parents to the offspring when both partners are unaffected carriers for the gene; the defect could be due to either mutation or deletion which ultimately results in reduced rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (α and β chains) that make up haemoglobin; this causes the formation of abnormal haemoglobin molecules resulting in anaemia; thalassemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia in that the former is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules, while the latter is a qualitative problem of synthesising an incorrectly functioning globin.
Given: HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ.
Formula/Principle: Monohybrid cross gives 1 : 2 : 1; independent events multiply; P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B).
Step 1: Offspring: ¼ HbᴬHbᴬ, ½ HbᴬHbˢ, ¼ HbˢHbˢ ⇒ P(affected) = 1/4.
Step 2: Independent births: (1/4)² = 1/16.
Step 3: Among normal children (¾), carriers are ½ ⇒ (1/2)/(3/4) = 2/3.
Why: Each birth is an independent event, and conditioning on a normal phenotype removes the affected class from the denominator.
Why not the others: (A) Probabilities and the amino acid change are wrong. (B) Two affected children is (1/4)²; thalassemia is quantitative. (D) Both disorders are autosomal.
Key point: Carrier × carrier: ¼ affected; normal child is a carrier with probability 2/3.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using salient facts of the Human Genome Project to calculate ratios and fractions — genome size, gene number, largest gene, protein-coding fraction, gene density on chromosomes 1 and Y, and SNPs
questions.question: The Human Genome Project found 3164.7 million bases, about 30,000 genes with an average gene length of 3000 bases, 2968 genes on chromosome 1 and 231 on chromosome Y. Which set of conclusions is correct?
options: A) The ratio of genes on chromosome 1 to Y is about 12.8; the largest known human gene, dystrophin, has 2.4 million bases; less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a large portion of the genome; and about 1.4 million locations with single-base differences (SNPs) were identified
B) The ratio of genes on chromosome 1 to Y is about 0.08; the largest gene has 3000 bases
C) More than 50 per cent of the genome codes for proteins, so there are about 10⁶ genes
D) Chromosome Y has the most genes because it determines sex
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ratio ≈ 12.8; dystrophin 2.4 Mb; < 2 % codes for proteins; many repeats; ~1.4 million SNPs.
Concept: The Human Genome Project (HGP) was called a mega project; some of the salient observations drawn from it are: the human genome contains 3164.7 million nucleotide bases; the average gene consists of 3000 bases, but sizes vary greatly, with the largest known human gene being dystrophin at 2.4 million bases; the total number of genes is estimated at 30,000 — much lower than previous estimates of 80,000 to 1,40,000 genes — and almost all (99.9 per cent) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all people; the functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes; less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a very large portion of the human genome; repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences that are repeated many times, sometimes hundreds to thousands of times, and are thought to have no direct coding functions, but they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution; chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968), and the Y has the fewest (231); scientists have identified about 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences (SNPs — single nucleotide polymorphism, pronounced as 'snips') occur in humans; this information promises to revolutionise the processes of finding chromosomal locations for disease-associated sequences and tracing human history.
Given: Genome 3164.7 Mb; 30,000 genes; chromosome 1: 2968 genes; Y: 231 genes.
Formula/Principle: Ratio = gene count on chromosome 1 ÷ gene count on Y.
Step 1: 2968/231 ≈ 12.8.
Step 2: Dystrophin 2.4 × 10⁶ bases ≈ 800 times the average gene length (3000 bases).
Step 3: Protein-coding fraction < 2 %; SNPs ≈ 1.4 × 10⁶.
Why: Gene lengths include long non-coding introns and the genome is rich in repeats, so the protein-coding part is a tiny fraction.
Why not the others: (B) Ratio inverted; dystrophin is the largest gene. (C) Less than 2 % codes for proteins; about 30,000 genes. (D) Y has the fewest genes.
Key point: 3164.7 Mb, ~30,000 genes, < 2 % coding; chromosome 1 most genes, Y fewest.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of steps in DNA fingerprinting using VNTR probes
questions.question: Which sequence of steps in DNA fingerprinting is correct?
options: A) Autoradiography → isolation of DNA → hybridisation → electrophoresis
B) Hybridisation with probe → digestion → isolation of DNA → blotting
C) Electrophoresis of intact chromosomes → staining with a VNTR → PCR

D) Isolation of DNA → digestion by restriction endonucleases → separation of fragments by electrophoresis → transfer (blotting) of separated fragments to synthetic membranes such as nitrocellulose or nylon → hybridisation using a labelled VNTR probe → detection of hybridised fragments by autoradiography; the VNTR (a satellite DNA showing high polymorphism) varies in copy number between individuals, so band sizes differ, and the technique is used in forensics and paternity testing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Isolation → restriction digestion → electrophoresis → Southern blotting → hybridisation with VNTR probe → autoradiography.
Concept: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions in DNA sequence called repetitive DNA, because in these sequences a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times; these repetitive DNA are separated from bulk genomic DNA as different peaks during density gradient centrifugation; the bulk DNA forms a major peak and the other small peaks are referred to as satellite DNA; depending on base composition (A:T rich or G:C rich), length of segment and number of repetitive units, the satellite DNA is classified into many categories, such as micro-satellites, mini-satellites etc.; these sequences normally do not code for any proteins, but they form a large portion of the human genome and show a high degree of polymorphism, forming the basis of DNA fingerprinting. The technique of DNA fingerprinting was initially developed by Alec Jeffreys; he used a satellite DNA as probe that shows a very high degree of polymorphism; it was called Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR). The technique, as used earlier, involved Southern blot hybridisation using radiolabelled VNTR as a probe; it included (i) isolation of DNA, (ii) digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases, (iii) separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis, (iv) transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes, such as nitrocellulose or nylon, (v) hybridisation using labelled VNTR probe, and (vi) detection of hybridised DNA fragments by autoradiography. The VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA referred to as mini-satellite; a small DNA sequence is arranged tandemly in many copy numbers; the copy number varies from chromosome to chromosome in an individual; the numbers of repeats show very high degree of polymorphism; as a result, the size of VNTR varies in size from 0.1 to 20 kb; consequently, after hybridisation with VNTR probe, the autoradiogram gives many bands of differing sizes; these bands give a characteristic pattern for an individual DNA.
Step 1: Isolate DNA and cut it with restriction enzymes.
Step 2: Separate fragments by electrophoresis; blot onto a membrane.
Step 3: Hybridise with labelled VNTR probe; detect by autoradiography.
Why: Fragments must be cut, size-separated and fixed on a membrane before a probe can locate the polymorphic VNTR sequences.
Why not the others: (A), (B) Steps out of order. (C) Chromosomes are not electrophoresed intact; the VNTR is the probe.
Key point: Isolate → digest → electrophoresis → blot → hybridise (VNTR) → autoradiograph.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing gene flow, genetic drift and mutation as factors that change allele frequencies, including the founder effect
questions.question: Which comparison of gene flow, genetic drift and mutation is correct?
options: A) Gene flow occurs by chance only in small populations, while drift requires migration

B) Gene flow (gene migration) changes allele frequencies when individuals move between populations, adding or removing alleles and tending to make populations more similar; genetic drift is a chance change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations, and when a few individuals found a new population the altered gene pool may make it a different species (founder effect); mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles, and mutations, recombination during gametogenesis and gene flow all create variation on which natural selection acts
C) Mutation removes alleles but never adds new ones
D) Genetic drift always increases the frequency of the most beneficial allele
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Gene flow by migration; drift by chance (founder effect); mutation as source of new alleles.
Concept: Five factors are known to affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population; new genes/alleles are added to the new population and these are lost from the old population; there would be a gene flow if this gene migration happens multiple times. If the same change occurs by chance, it is called genetic drift; sometimes the change in allele frequency is so different in the new sample of population that they become a different species; the original drifted population becomes founders and the effect is called the founder effect. Microbial experiments show that pre-existing advantageous mutations when selected will result in observation of new phenotypes; over a few generations, this would result in speciation; natural selection is a process in which heritable variations enabling better survival are enabled to reproduce and leave a greater number of progeny; variation due to mutation or variation due to recombination during gametogenesis, or due to gene flow or genetic drift results in changed frequency of genes and alleles in future generations.
Why: Each factor alters allele frequencies by a different route — movement of individuals, random sampling, or new changes in DNA.
Why not the others: (A) Definitions swapped. (C) Mutation creates new alleles. (D) Drift is random, not directed.
Key point: Gene flow (migration), drift (chance, founder effect), mutation (new alleles).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the idea of adaptive radiation to a case of island colonisation, distinguishing it from convergent evolution, and placing events of human evolution in time
questions.question: A single seed-eating bird species colonises an isolated group of islands. After a long time, the islands have many related species with beaks for seeds, insects or nectar. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) This is adaptive radiation: evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats, as in Darwin's finches of the Galapagos and the Australian marsupials; when adaptive radiation in isolated areas produces similar forms in different lineages (such as placental and marsupial wolves), it is convergent evolution; in human evolution, Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus lived about 15 mya, Australopithecines about 2 mya, modern Homo sapiens arose about 75,000–10,000 years ago during the ice age, prehistoric cave art developed about 18,000 years ago, and agriculture began about 10,000 years ago
B) This is convergent evolution because all species descend from one ancestor
C) The changes happened because birds used their beaks more, as Lamarck proposed, and humans evolved from Neanderthals only 1000 years ago
D) Island species are identical to their ancestor because isolation prevents change
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Adaptive radiation (finches, marsupials); convergence when different lineages produce similar forms; human evolution timeline.
Concept: During his journey Darwin went to the Galapagos Islands; there he observed an amazing diversity of creatures; of particular interest, small black birds (later called Darwin's finches) amazed him; he realised that there were many varieties of finches in the same island; all the varieties, he conjectured, evolved on the island itself; from the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches; this process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats) is called adaptive radiation. Another example is Australian marsupials: a number of marsupials, each different from the other, evolved from an ancestral stock, but all within the Australian island continent; when more than one adaptive radiation appeared to have occurred in an isolated geographical area (representing different habitats), one can call this convergent evolution; placental mammals in Australia also exhibit adaptive radiation in evolving into varieties of such placental mammals each of which appears to be 'similar' to a corresponding marsupial (e.g. placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf-marsupial). About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were existing; two million years ago, Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands; the first human-like being, the hominid, was called Homo habilis, with brain capacities between 650–800 cc; fossils discovered in Java in 1891 revealed the next stage, Homo erectus about 1.5 mya, with a large brain around 900 cc; the Neanderthal man with a brain size of 1400 cc lived in near east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000–40,000 years back; Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents; during the ice age between 75,000–10,000 years ago modern Homo sapiens arose; pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago; agriculture came around 10,000 years back and human settlements started.
Why: Different islands offer different food sources, so descendants of one colonising species diversify to exploit them.
Why not the others: (B) Diversification from one ancestor is divergent (adaptive radiation); convergence produces similar forms in different lineages. (C) Lamarckian use-and-disuse is not accepted; human timeline wrong. (D) Isolation promotes divergence.
Key point: Adaptive radiation = divergence from one ancestor; convergent evolution = similar forms in different lineages.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the cause of the recurring fever in malaria and the transmission and effects of amoebiasis, ascariasis, filariasis and ringworm
questions.question: Which explanation of these diseases is correct?
options: A) Malaria fever is caused by mosquito saliva, and ringworm by a roundworm
B) Filariasis is caused by a fungus that blocks blood vessels

C) In malaria, the rupture of RBCs releases a toxic substance, haemozoin, which causes the chills and high fever recurring every three to four days; amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica) spreads through food and water contaminated with faeces, with houseflies as mechanical carriers; Ascaris eggs pass out with faeces and infect through contaminated water, vegetables and fruits; Wuchereria, transmitted by the bite of female mosquito vectors, causes chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs (elephantiasis); ringworm is caused by fungi of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton, with heat and moisture helping them grow
D) Amoebiasis is transmitted by the bite of female Anopheles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Haemozoin from ruptured RBCs causes recurring fever; transmission and effects of the other diseases as described.
Concept: Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form) through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito; the parasites initially multiply within the liver cells and then attack the red blood cells (RBCs), resulting in their rupture; the rupture of RBCs is associated with release of a toxic substance, haemozoin, which is responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of human which causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery); symptoms of this disease include constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucous and blood clots; houseflies act as mechanical carriers and serve to transmit the parasite from faeces of an infected person to food and food products, thereby contaminating them; drinking water and food contaminated by the faecal matter are the main source of infection. Ascaris, the common round worm, is an intestinal parasite causing ascariasis; symptoms include internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anemia and blockage of the intestinal passage; the eggs of the parasite are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons, which contaminate soil, water, plants etc.; a healthy person acquires this infection through contaminated water, vegetables, fruits etc. Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi), the filarial worms, cause a slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs in which they live for many years, usually the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs, and the disease is called elephantiasis or filariasis; the pathogens are transmitted to a healthy person through the bite by the female mosquito vectors. Many fungi belonging to the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are responsible for ringworms; appearance of dry, scaly lesions on various parts of the body such as skin, nails and scalp are the main symptoms, accompanied by intense itching; heat and moisture help these fungi to grow, which makes them thrive in skin folds such as those in the groin or between the toes; ringworms are generally acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected individuals.
Why: Each pathogen's life cycle decides how it spreads and why symptoms appear, such as synchronised RBC rupture causing periodic fever.
Why not the others: (A) Fever is caused by haemozoin; ringworm is fungal. (B) Filariasis is caused by a nematode. (D) Amoebiasis spreads by contaminated food and water.
Key point: Malaria fever: haemozoin; amoebiasis: houseflies; filariasis: female mosquito; ringworm: fungi.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of steps for selecting recombinants when a gene is inserted at the PstI site within the ampicillin-resistance gene of pBR322
questions.question: A gene is inserted into the PstI site, which lies within the ampicillin resistance gene (ampᴿ) of plasmid pBR322; the tetracycline resistance gene (tetᴿ) remains intact. Which sequence of steps identifies the recombinants?
options: A) Plate transformants on ampicillin, pick colonies that grow and discard those that die on tetracycline
B) Recombinants grow on both antibiotics, so no replica plating is needed
C) Transformants are selected only by blue colour on X-gal

D) Transform E. coli with the ligation mixture → plate on tetracycline medium, on which all transformants (recombinant or not) grow while non-transformed cells die → replica-plate the colonies onto ampicillin medium → colonies that fail to grow on ampicillin but grew on tetracycline are recombinants, because the inserted DNA has inactivated ampᴿ (insertional inactivation)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Transform → select on tetracycline → replica plate on ampicillin → recombinants are tetracycline-resistant but ampicillin-sensitive.
Concept: A vector requires a selectable marker, which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants; normally, the genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli; the normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against any of these antibiotics. In order to link the alien DNA, the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes; the ligation of alien DNA is carried out at a restriction site present in one of the two antibiotic resistance genes; for example, you can ligate a foreign DNA at the BamHI site of the tetracycline resistance gene in the vector pBR322; the recombinant plasmids will lose tetracycline resistance due to insertion of foreign DNA but can still be selected out from non-recombinants by plating the transformants on ampicillin containing medium; the transformants growing on ampicillin containing medium are then transferred on a medium containing tetracycline; the recombinants will grow in ampicillin containing medium but not on that containing tetracycline, but non-recombinants will grow on the medium containing both the antibiotics. In this case, one antibiotic resistance gene helps in selecting the transformants, whereas the other antibiotic resistance gene gets 'inactivated due to insertion' of alien DNA, and helps in selection of recombinants. pBR322 also has a PstI site within the ampᴿ gene; insertion there inactivates ampᴿ instead, so the roles of the two antibiotics are interchanged.
Step 1: Transform E. coli; plate on tetracycline (intact marker) ⇒ only transformants grow.
Step 2: Replica plate on ampicillin.
Step 3: No growth on ampicillin ⇒ ampᴿ inactivated ⇒ recombinant.
Why: The intact resistance gene selects cells carrying any plasmid, while loss of the interrupted resistance gene marks plasmids with an insert.
Why not the others: (A) Uses the inactivated marker for primary selection, so recombinants would die. (B) Recombinants lose ampicillin resistance. (C) pBR322 does not carry lacZ for blue–white screening.
Key point: Insert in ampᴿ: select on tetracycline, screen for loss of ampicillin resistance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing gene therapy for adenosine deaminase deficiency with stem-cell-based approaches, including why lymphocyte gene therapy needs repeated infusions and how a permanent cure could be achieved
questions.question: Which comparison of gene therapy and stem-cell approaches is correct?
options: A) Gene therapy changes the patient's diet so that ADA is no longer needed

B) Gene therapy corrects a gene defect by delivering a normal gene into a person's cells or tissues; in ADA deficiency, the patient's lymphocytes are grown in culture, a functional ADA cDNA is introduced with a retroviral vector, and the cells are returned, but because these cells are not immortal the patient needs periodic infusions; introducing the gene into bone marrow stem cells at early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure, because stem cells can divide indefinitely and differentiate into specialised cells, so they keep producing corrected blood cells; stem-cell therapy aims to replace damaged tissue using such self-renewing cells
C) Mature lymphocytes are stem cells, so one infusion is a permanent cure
D) Enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy are identical because both supply the ADA gene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Gene therapy delivers a normal gene; lymphocyte therapy needs repeated infusions; gene transfer into stem cells could cure permanently.
Concept: If a person is born with a hereditary disease, can a corrective therapy be taken for such a disease? Gene therapy is an attempt to do this; gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child/embryo; here genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease; correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of and compensate for the non-functional gene. The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; this enzyme is crucial for the immune system to function; the disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase; in some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection; but the problem with both of these approaches is that they are not completely curative. As a first step towards gene therapy, lymphocytes from the blood of the patient are grown in a culture outside the body; a functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is then introduced into these lymphocytes, which are subsequently returned to the patient; however, as these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes; however, if the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure. Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide repeatedly (self-renew) and give rise to specialised cell types, which is why corrected stem cells could keep supplying healthy cells.
Why: A cure lasts only as long as the corrected cells keep dividing; mature lymphocytes have limited life, whereas stem cells self-renew.
Why not the others: (A) Gene therapy delivers a gene, not a diet. (C) Mature lymphocytes are not stem cells. (D) Enzyme replacement injects the protein, not the gene.
Key point: Gene therapy delivers a normal gene; stem cells self-renew, so correcting them could cure permanently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting field observations on biological control of an introduced plant, removal of a keystone predator, prey defences and brood parasitism
questions.question: (i) Prickly pear cactus spread uncontrollably after introduction into Australia, until a cactus-feeding moth from its native range was introduced. (ii) When all starfish Pisaster were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than ten species of invertebrates became extinct within a year. (iii) Birds avoid eating Monarch butterflies. (iv) Crows unknowingly incubate cuckoo eggs. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (i) The moth is a parasite of the cactus, and (ii) starfish remove competitors that help other invertebrates
B) (iii) Monarchs are distasteful because they produce the poison themselves from birth
C) (iv) The cuckoo is a predator of crows

D) (i) An introduced species spreads fast without its natural predator, and introducing a predator (here a herbivore) controlled it, the basis of biological control; (ii) Pisaster acts as a predator that keeps prey populations under control and reduces competition among them, so its removal led to competitive exclusion and loss of species; (iii) Monarchs are distasteful because the caterpillar feeds on a poisonous weed and stores the chemical; (iv) the cuckoo is a brood parasite whose eggs resemble the host's eggs in size and colour
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Biological control; predator maintains diversity by reducing competition; acquired chemical defence; brood parasitism.
Concept: Predators play other important roles besides acting as 'conduits' for energy transfer: they keep prey populations under control; but for predators, prey species could achieve very high population densities and cause ecosystem instability; when certain exotic species are introduced into a geographical area, they become invasive and start spreading fast because the invaded land does not have its natural predators; the prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s caused havoc by spreading rapidly into millions of hectares of rangeland; finally, the invasive cactus was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced into the country; biological control methods adopted in agricultural pest control are based on the ability of the predator to regulate the prey population. Predators also help in maintaining species diversity in a community, by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species; in the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast the starfish Pisaster is an important predator; in a field experiment, when all the starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year, because of interspecific competition. The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator (bird) because of a special chemical present in its body; interestingly, the butterfly acquires this chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed. Brood parasitism in birds is a fascinating example of parasitism in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them; during the course of evolution, the eggs of the parasitic bird have evolved to resemble the host's egg in size and colour to reduce the chances of the host bird detecting the foreign eggs and ejecting them from the nest; try to follow the movements of the cuckoo (koel) and the crow in your neighbourhood park during the breeding season (spring to summer) and watch brood parasitism in action.
Why: Predation and parasitism regulate populations and community structure, and both drive the evolution of defences and counter-adaptations.
Why not the others: (A) The moth acts as a predator (herbivore); starfish reduce competition among prey. (B) The chemical is acquired from food. (C) The cuckoo is a brood parasite.
Key point: Predators control prey and maintain diversity; brood parasites mimic host eggs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating gross and net primary productivity and secondary productivity from incident radiation, photosynthetic efficiency and respiration, and comparing ocean and land productivity
questions.question: A crop field receives 1.0 × 10⁶ kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ of sunlight, of which 50 % is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR). Plants fix 2 % of the PAR as gross primary productivity (GPP) and use 40 % of GPP in respiration. Herbivores convert 10 % of the net primary productivity (NPP) into their own biomass. What are the GPP, NPP and secondary productivity, and which statement is correct?
options: A) GPP 2.0 × 10⁴, NPP 1.2 × 10⁴, secondary 1200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; oceans contribute most of the biosphere's productivity

B) GPP 1.0 × 10⁴, NPP 6.0 × 10³, secondary 600 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; NPP is the biomass available to heterotrophs, secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers, and although oceans cover about 70 % of the surface, their annual NPP (about 55 billion tons) is less than that of land (about 115 billion tons) out of about 170 billion tons in all
C) GPP 5.0 × 10⁵, NPP 3.0 × 10⁵, secondary 3.0 × 10⁴ kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹
D) GPP 1.0 × 10⁴, NPP 4.0 × 10³, secondary 400 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; respiration losses are added to GPP to give NPP
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) GPP 1.0 × 10⁴, NPP 6.0 × 10³, secondary 600 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; oceans less productive than land overall.
Concept: A constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain; primary production is defined as the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis; it is expressed in terms of weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²); the rate of biomass production is called productivity, expressed in terms of g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or (kcal m⁻²) yr⁻¹ to compare the productivity of different ecosystems; it can be divided into gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP); gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis; a considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants in respiration; gross primary productivity minus respiration losses (R) is the net primary productivity (NPP): GPP − R = NPP; net primary productivity is the available biomass for the consumption of heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers); secondary productivity is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers. Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting a particular area; it also depends on a variety of environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity of plants; therefore, it varies in different types of ecosystems; the annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately 170 billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter; of this, despite occupying about 70 per cent of the surface, the productivity of the oceans is only 55 billion tons. Of the incident solar radiation less than 50 per cent of it is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR); plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the PAR and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.
Given: Sunlight 1.0 × 10⁶ kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; PAR 50 %; efficiency 2 %; R = 40 % GPP; herbivore conversion 10 %.
Formula/Principle: GPP = efficiency × PAR; NPP = GPP − R; secondary productivity = conversion × NPP.
Step 1: PAR = 5.0 × 10⁵; GPP = 0.02 × 5.0 × 10⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁴ kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Step 2: NPP = 1.0 × 10⁴ − 0.4 × 1.0 × 10⁴ = 6.0 × 10³ kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Step 3: Secondary = 0.10 × 6.0 × 10³ = 600 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Why: Only a small fraction of sunlight is fixed, part is used by the plant itself, and only a fraction of what remains is built into consumer biomass.
Why not the others: (A) PAR step omitted; oceans produce less than land. (C) Uses PAR as GPP. (D) Respiration subtracted wrongly (60 %); NPP = GPP − R.
Key point: GPP − R = NPP; oceans ~55 of ~170 billion tons despite 70 % area.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of consequences in Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper analogy for species loss, Tilman's experimental findings on diversity and stability, and the three reasons to conserve biodiversity
questions.question: Which sequence and description about the importance of biodiversity is correct?
options: A) Removing any one species immediately causes collapse of the whole ecosystem, so all species are equally important
B) Tilman found that plots with fewer species had more stable biomass from year to year

C) In Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis an ecosystem is compared to an aeroplane and species to rivets → removing a few rivets (species) may not affect flight (ecosystem function) at first → as more rivets are removed the plane becomes dangerously weak over time → loss of rivets on key parts, like the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions), is more serious than loss of a few rivets on seats; Tilman's long-term outdoor plots showed that plots with more species varied less in total biomass from year to year and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity; biodiversity is conserved for narrowly utilitarian (food, fibre, medicines), broadly utilitarian (ecosystem services such as the Amazon producing about 20 % of Earth's oxygen through photosynthesis, pollination) and ethical reasons
D) Biodiversity is valued only for the commercial products it provides
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rivet popper sequence; Tilman: diversity → stability and productivity; narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons.
Concept: Communities with more species, generally, tend to be more stable than those with less species; a stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year; it must be either resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and it must also be resistant to invasions by alien species. David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots provide some tentative answers: he found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass; he also showed that in his experiments, increased diversity contributed to higher productivity. Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich used an analogy to understand the contribution of species richness: in an airplane (ecosystem) all parts are joined together using thousands of rivets (species); if every passenger travelling in it starts popping a rivet to take home (causing a species to become extinct), it may not affect flight safety (proper functioning of the ecosystem) initially, but as more and more rivets are removed, the plane becomes dangerously weak over a period of time; furthermore, which rivet is removed may also be critical; loss of rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is obviously a more serious threat to flight safety than loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane. The reasons for conservation can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, and ethical; the narrowly utilitarian arguments for conserving biodiversity are obvious — humans derive countless direct economic benefits from nature: food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and products of medicinal importance; the broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides — the fast-dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere; pollination is another service; the ethical argument relates to what we owe to millions of plant, animal and microbe species with whom we share this planet.
Step 1: A few species lost ⇒ little immediate effect.
Step 2: Continued loss ⇒ progressive weakening.
Step 3: Loss of key species ⇒ disproportionate damage.
Why: Ecosystem function depends both on the number of species and on which species are lost, since some drive major processes.
Why not the others: (A) Early losses may have little effect, and species differ in importance. (B) More species gave more stable biomass. (D) Broadly utilitarian and ethical reasons also apply.
Key point: Rivet popper: gradual weakening, key species critical; diversity → stability (Tilman).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the biological species concept to cases of interbreeding and sterile hybrids, and distinguishing taxonomy from systematics
questions.question: (i) Two populations of frogs look almost identical but, when brought together, never interbreed. (ii) A horse and a donkey mate to produce a mule, which is sterile. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (i) The two populations are separate species, because a species is a group of individuals that can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring and are reproductively isolated from other groups; (ii) horses and donkeys are separate species because their hybrid is sterile; taxonomy involves characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature, while systematics also takes evolutionary relationships between organisms into account
B) (i) They are one species because they look alike
C) (ii) Horses and donkeys are one species because they can mate
D) Taxonomy and systematics mean exactly the same, and neither considers evolution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Reproductive isolation defines species; sterile hybrids show separate species; systematics adds evolutionary relationships.
Concept: Taxonomic studies consider a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities as a species; one should be able to distinguish one species from the other closely related species based on the distinct morphological differences; biologically, all living organisms of a species are able to interbreed among themselves and produce fertile offspring, and members of different species are reproductively isolated from each other. In such cases, appearance alone may mislead: populations that look alike but do not interbreed are separate species, and organisms of different species that mate may produce sterile hybrids, such as the mule. Characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature are the processes that are basic to taxonomy; taxonomy is not something new; human beings have always been interested in knowing more and more about the various kinds of organisms; the word systematics is derived from the Latin word 'systema' which means systematic arrangement of organisms; Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication; the scope of systematics was later enlarged to include identification, nomenclature and classification; systematics takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms.
Why: Reproductive isolation, not appearance, keeps the gene pools of species separate.
Why not the others: (B) Appearance does not decide species membership. (C) Mating alone is not enough; offspring must be fertile. (D) Systematics includes evolutionary relationships.
Key point: Species = interbreeding, fertile offspring, reproductively isolated; systematics includes evolutionary relationships.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Arranging samples of different substances in order of the total number of atoms using the mole concept and molar masses
questions.question: Arrange the following in decreasing order of the total number of atoms: (P) 4.0 g of He, (Q) 1.0 g of H₂, (R) 9.0 g of H₂O, (S) 8.0 g of O₃, (T) 0.50 mol of NH₃. (Molar masses: He 4, H₂ 2, H₂O 18, O₃ 48, NH₃ 17 g mol⁻¹.)
options: A) P > Q > R > S > T
B) T > R > P = Q > S
C) R > T > P > Q > S
D) S > R > T > P = Q
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) T (2 mol atoms) > R (1.5) > P = Q (1) > S (0.5).
Concept: One mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many particles or entities as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of the carbon-12 isotope; this number, 6.022 × 10²³, is the Avogadro constant. The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is called its molar mass, numerically equal to its atomic, molecular or formula mass in u. Number of moles = given mass/molar mass; the number of atoms in a molecular substance equals (moles of molecules) × (atoms per molecule) × Nₐ. Comparing moles of atoms is therefore equivalent to comparing numbers of atoms, since Nₐ is common.
Given: Masses and molar masses above; 0.50 mol NH₃.
Formula/Principle: moles of atoms = (mass/M) × atoms per formula unit.
Step 1: P: 4.0/4 = 1.0 mol He atoms; Q: 1.0/2 = 0.50 mol H₂ × 2 = 1.0 mol atoms.
Step 2: R: 9.0/18 = 0.50 mol × 3 = 1.5 mol atoms; S: 8.0/48 = 1/6 mol × 3 = 0.50 mol atoms.
Step 3: T: 0.50 mol × 4 = 2.0 mol atoms ⇒ T > R > P = Q > S.
Why: Equal masses do not mean equal atoms; both molar mass and atomicity matter.
Why not the others: (A) Ranks by mass, not atoms. (C) Undercounts NH₃'s four atoms. (D) Treats O₃ as having more atoms because of its mass.
Key point: Atoms = (m/M) × atomicity × Nₐ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the results of Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment, why they disproved Thomson's model, and the limitation of the nuclear model
questions.question: In Rutherford's experiment, a beam of α-particles was directed at a very thin gold foil. Most particles passed through undeflected, a small fraction were deflected by small angles, and very few (about 1 in 20,000) bounced nearly straight back. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The results support Thomson's model, in which positive charge is spread uniformly through the atom
B) Most of the atom's mass is in the electrons, which deflect the α-particles
C) The nucleus occupies about half the atom's volume

D) Most of the atom is empty space; the positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus (radius about 10⁻¹⁵ m, compared with about 10⁻¹⁰ m for the atom), which repels the few α-particles that approach it closely; Thomson's uniform-charge model could not produce large deflections; but Rutherford's model could not explain atomic stability, because an orbiting electron is accelerating and should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mostly empty space; tiny dense positive nucleus; Thomson model fails; Rutherford model cannot explain stability.
Concept: Rutherford and his students (Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden) bombarded very thin gold foil with α-particles; a stream of high energy α-particles from a radioactive source was directed at a thin foil (thickness about 100 nm) of gold metal; the thin gold foil had a circular fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around it; whenever α-particles struck the screen, a tiny flash of light was produced at that point. The results were quite unexpected: according to Thomson's model of the atom, the mass of each gold atom in the foil should have been spread evenly over the entire atom, and α-particles had enough energy to pass directly through such a uniform distribution of mass; it was expected that the particles would slow down and change directions only by small angles as they passed through the foil; it was observed that (i) most of the α-particles passed through the gold foil undeflected, (ii) a small fraction of the α-particles was deflected by small angles, and (iii) a very few α-particles (∼1 in 20,000) bounced back, that is, were deflected by nearly 180°. On the basis of the observations, Rutherford drew the following conclusions: most of the space in the atom is empty as most of the α-particles passed through the foil undeflected; a few positively charged α-particles were deflected — the deflection must be due to enormous repulsive force showing that the positive charge of the atom is not spread throughout the atom as Thomson had presumed; the positive charge has to be concentrated in a very small volume that repelled and deflected the positively charged α-particles; calculations by Rutherford showed that the volume occupied by the nucleus is negligibly small as compared to the total volume of the atom; the radius of the atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m, while that of the nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m. According to the electromagnetic theory of Maxwell, charged particles when accelerated should emit electromagnetic radiation; an electron in an orbit will emit radiation, the energy carried by radiation comes from electronic motion, and the orbit will continue to shrink; calculations show that it should take an electron only 10⁻⁸ s to spiral into the nucleus — Rutherford's model therefore cannot explain the stability of an atom.
Step 1: Most undeflected ⇒ mostly empty space.
Step 2: Rare large-angle deflection ⇒ tiny region of concentrated positive charge and mass.
Step 3: Accelerating electrons should radiate ⇒ model cannot explain stability.
Why: Only a concentrated charge produces fields strong enough to turn an energetic α-particle back.
Why not the others: (A) A uniform charge gives only small deflections. (B) Electrons are far too light to deflect α-particles strongly. (C) The nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's volume scale.
Key point: Tiny dense nucleus; Rutherford model cannot explain stability.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Explaining why chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, why noble gases have positive values, why adding a second electron to O⁻ is endothermic, and how electronegativity differs from electron gain enthalpy
