questions.question: Chlorine's electron gain enthalpy is −349 kJ mol⁻¹ while fluorine's is −328 kJ mol⁻¹, noble gases have positive values, and O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) absorbs energy. Which explanation of these facts, and of electronegativity, is correct?
options: A) Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine because an electron added to the small, compact 2p subshell of fluorine suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already present; noble gases have large positive electron gain enthalpies because the electron must enter the next higher shell; adding an electron to O⁻ is endothermic because it is repelled by the negative ion; electronegativity is a qualitative measure of an atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond, not a measurable energy, and fluorine has the highest value
B) Fluorine has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements because it is the most electronegative
C) Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity are the same measurable quantity
D) The second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen is more negative than the first
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cl > F in magnitude due to repulsion in compact 2p; noble gases positive; O⁻ + e⁻ endothermic; electronegativity is qualitative, F highest.
Concept: When an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom (X) to convert it into a negative ion, the enthalpy change accompanying the process is defined as the electron gain enthalpy (ΔegH); depending on the element, the process of adding an electron to the atom can be either endothermic or exothermic; for many elements energy is released when an electron is added. Group 17 elements (the halogens) have very high negative electron gain enthalpies because they can attain a stable noble gas electronic configuration by picking up an electron; on the other hand, noble gases have large positive electron gain enthalpies because the electron has to enter the next higher principal quantum level, leading to a very unstable electronic configuration. Electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative as we go down a group because the size of the atom increases and the added electron would be farther from the nucleus; this is generally the case; however, electron gain enthalpy of O or F is less negative than that of the succeeding element; this is because when an electron is added to O or F, the added electron goes to the smaller n = 2 quantum level and suffers significant repulsion from the other electrons present in this level; for the n = 3 quantum level (S or Cl), the added electron occupies a larger region of space and the electron–electron repulsion is much less. Adding a second electron to a negative ion such as O⁻ requires energy because the incoming electron is repelled by the negative charge. A qualitative measure of the ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself is called electronegativity; unlike ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy, it is not a measurable quantity; however, a number of numerical scales of electronegativity of elements, viz. the Pauling scale, have been developed; on the Pauling scale fluorine, the most electronegative element, is assigned a value of 4.0.
Why: The energy released when an electron is added depends on how strongly it is attracted and how much it is repelled by electrons already present.
Why not the others: (B) Chlorine's value is more negative. (C) Electronegativity is not a measured energy. (D) The second step is endothermic.
Key point: ΔegH(Cl) more negative than F; noble gases positive; electronegativity is qualitative.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking the energy steps in forming an ionic solid such as NaCl to its stability, and comparing lattice enthalpies of NaCl and MgO
questions.question: Which statement about the formation of NaCl and the lattice enthalpies of ionic solids is correct?
options: A) Forming Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g) from Na(g) and Cl(g) releases energy, so lattice enthalpy is not needed for stability
B) NaCl is stable because sodium's ionisation enthalpy is negative

C) Forming the ion pair Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) from gaseous atoms is endothermic overall (ionisation enthalpy of Na, +495.8 kJ mol⁻¹, exceeds the energy released in electron gain by Cl, −348.7 kJ mol⁻¹), so the stability of NaCl comes mainly from the large energy released when gaseous ions pack into the crystal lattice (lattice enthalpy, 788 kJ mol⁻¹); MgO has a much higher lattice enthalpy than NaCl because its ions carry charges of +2 and −2, and lattice enthalpies can be found indirectly by a Born–Haber cycle
D) MgO has a lower lattice enthalpy than NaCl because Mg is heavier
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ion-pair formation endothermic; lattice enthalpy (788 kJ mol⁻¹) gives stability; MgO higher due to 2+/2− charges; Born–Haber cycle.
Concept: The formation of an ionic compound would primarily depend upon the ease of formation of the positive and negative ions from the respective neutral atoms and the arrangement of the positive and negative ions in the solid, that is, the lattice of the crystalline compound. The formation of a positive ion involves ionisation, i.e. removal of electron(s) from the neutral atom, and that of the negative ion involves the addition of electron(s) to the neutral atom; ionisation enthalpy is always positive, and the sum of the electron gain enthalpy and the ionisation enthalpy may be positive, but still the crystal structure gets stabilised due to the energy released in the formation of the crystal lattice; for example, the ionisation enthalpy for Na⁺ formation from Na(g) is 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹, while the electron gain enthalpy for the change Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) is −348.7 kJ mol⁻¹ only; the sum of the two, 147.1 kJ mol⁻¹, is more than compensated for by the enthalpy of lattice formation of NaCl(s) (−788 kJ mol⁻¹); therefore, the energy released in the processes is more than the energy absorbed; thus a qualitative measure of the stability of an ionic compound is provided by its enthalpy of lattice formation and not simply by achieving octet of electrons around the ionic species in the gaseous state. The lattice enthalpy of an ionic solid is defined as the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions; it increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic size; it cannot be determined directly by experiment, so an indirect method using the Born–Haber cycle is used.
Why: The strong electrostatic attraction of many oppositely charged ions in a lattice releases enough energy to outweigh the cost of forming the ions.
Why not the others: (A) Ion-pair formation is endothermic. (B) Ionisation enthalpy is always positive. (D) Higher ionic charges in MgO give a larger lattice enthalpy.
Key point: Lattice enthalpy stabilises ionic solids; it increases with ionic charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining types of thermodynamic systems, state and path functions, the IUPAC sign convention for work, and work in free expansion
questions.question: A student classifies systems and quantities and applies the first law to a gas expanding into an evacuated vessel. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Heat q and work w are state functions, and internal energy depends on the path
B) A thermos flask containing hot tea is an open system
C) Free expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum requires the most work because no pressure opposes it

D) In an open system both matter and energy can be exchanged with the surroundings, in a closed system only energy, and in an isolated system neither; internal energy U, enthalpy H, pressure, volume and temperature are state functions, depending only on the state, while q and w depend on the path; by the IUPAC convention w is positive when work is done on the system and q is positive when heat is absorbed by it, so ΔU = q + w; when an ideal gas expands into a vacuum (p_ext = 0), w = 0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Open/closed/isolated systems; U, H, p, V, T state functions; q, w path functions; ΔU = q + w with IUPAC signs; free expansion w = 0.
Concept: In thermodynamics, the part of the universe under observation is called the system and the rest is the surroundings. In an open system, there is exchange of energy and matter between system and surroundings (e.g. reactants in an open beaker); in a closed system, there is no exchange of matter, but exchange of energy is possible (e.g. reactants in a closed vessel of conducting material); in an isolated system, there is no exchange of energy or matter (e.g. reactants in a thermos flask or any other closed insulated vessel). A system is described by state variables such as p, V, T and amount; a state function is one whose value depends only on the state of the system and not on how that state is reached — internal energy U and enthalpy H are state functions, as are p, V and T. Heat (q) and work (w) are not state functions, since their values depend on the path by which a change is carried out. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = q + w; by the sign convention, w is positive when work is done on the system and negative when work is done by the system, and q is positive when heat is transferred from the surroundings to the system. Expansion of a gas in vacuum (p_ext = 0) is called free expansion; no work is done during free expansion of an ideal gas whether the process is reversible or irreversible.
Why: State functions record only where the system is, whereas heat and work record how it got there.
Why not the others: (A) Roles reversed. (B) A thermos flask approximates an isolated system. (C) With no opposing pressure, w = 0.
Key point: ΔU = q + w; U, H state functions; free expansion w = 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using Le Chatelier's principle to predict the effect of pressure, temperature, concentration, a catalyst and an inert gas on the ammonia synthesis equilibrium
questions.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹, which set of predictions is correct?
options: A) Raising temperature increases K and the yield of NH₃

B) Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards NH₃ (fewer gas moles); raising temperature shifts it towards N₂ and H₂ and lowers K because the forward reaction is exothermic; removing NH₃ shifts it forward; a catalyst (iron with molybdenum) speeds attainment of equilibrium without changing its position or K; adding argon at constant volume does not change the partial pressures of the reactants and products, so the equilibrium does not shift
C) A catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of NH₃
D) Adding argon at constant volume shifts the equilibrium towards NH₃
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pressure ↑ favours NH₃; T ↑ favours reactants and lowers K; removing NH₃ shifts right; catalyst no shift; inert gas at constant V no effect.
Concept: Le Chatelier's principle states that a change in any of the factors that determine the equilibrium conditions of a system will cause the system to change in such a manner so as to reduce or to counteract the effect of the change. Increasing the concentration of a reactant or removing a product shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction. A pressure change obtained by changing the volume affects the yield of products in a gaseous reaction where the total number of moles of gaseous reactants and products differ; on increasing pressure, the reaction goes in the direction in which the number of moles of gas is reduced. Temperature changes alter the value of the equilibrium constant: for an exothermic reaction (negative ΔH), K decreases as temperature increases; for an endothermic reaction, K increases with temperature; production of ammonia according to the reaction is an exothermic process, so according to Le Chatelier's principle raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left and decreases the equilibrium concentration of ammonia. A catalyst increases the rate of the chemical reaction by making available a new low-energy pathway for the conversion of reactants to products; it increases the rate of forward and reverse reactions that pass through the same transition state and does not affect equilibrium; in the Haber process, iron oxide with a small amount of K₂O and Al₂O₃ (or molybdenum as promoter) is used. If the volume is kept constant and an inert gas such as argon is added, which does not take part in the reaction, the equilibrium remains undisturbed, because the addition of an inert gas at constant volume does not change the partial pressures or the molar concentrations of the substances involved in the reaction.
Why: The system responds to any imposed change by shifting in the direction that partly offsets it, while a catalyst only speeds both directions equally.
Why not the others: (A) Exothermic reaction: K falls on heating. (C) A catalyst does not change the yield at equilibrium. (D) Partial pressures are unchanged at constant volume.
Key point: Le Chatelier: pressure → fewer gas moles; heat → endothermic direction; catalyst and inert gas (constant V) no shift.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the concentration of Fe²⁺ from a permanganate titration, explaining why KMnO₄ acts as its own indicator, and classifying types of redox reactions
questions.question: 25.0 mL of an acidified Fe²⁺ solution needs 20.0 mL of 0.020 M KMnO₄ to reach a permanent pale pink colour. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 0.080 M, because MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, so 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol MnO₄⁻ oxidises 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol Fe²⁺; KMnO₄ is a self-indicator because the first slight excess of intensely coloured MnO₄⁻ turns the colourless solution pink; redox reactions include combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation reactions, such as 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, in which oxygen is both oxidised and reduced
B) 0.016 M, because one MnO₄⁻ reacts with one Fe²⁺
C) 0.40 M; an external indicator such as phenolphthalein is required
D) 0.080 M; in the reaction Mn changes from +7 to +4, and disproportionation means two different elements are oxidised
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.080 M; KMnO₄ self-indicator; types of redox reactions.
Concept: Redox titrations use an oxidising agent to estimate a reducing agent (or vice versa); in acidic medium permanganate is reduced from Mn(+7) to Mn²⁺(+2), gaining five electrons, while each Fe²⁺ loses one electron to become Fe³⁺, so one MnO₄⁻ oxidises five Fe²⁺. In the titration of Fe²⁺ with MnO₄⁻, the intense purple colour of MnO₄⁻ disappears as long as Fe²⁺ remains; the first excess drop imparts a pink colour to the solution, so MnO₄⁻ acts as a self indicator; the visible end point is achieved after the reductant has been completely consumed. Redox reactions can be divided into combination reactions (two or more substances combine), decomposition reactions (a compound breaks down), displacement reactions (an ion or atom in a compound is replaced by an ion or atom of another element), and disproportionation reactions, in which an element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), where oxygen in the −1 state goes to −2 in water and 0 in O₂.
Given: V(Fe²⁺) = 25.0 mL; V(KMnO₄) = 20.0 mL of 0.020 M.
Formula/Principle: n(Fe²⁺) = 5 × n(MnO₄⁻).
Step 1: n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.020 × 0.0200 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Step 2: n(Fe²⁺) = 5 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol.
Step 3: [Fe²⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻³/0.0250 = 0.080 M.
Why: Electron balance fixes the 1 : 5 ratio, and the coloured oxidant signals its own excess.
Why not the others: (B) Ignores the 5-electron change. (C) Wrong arithmetic; no external indicator needed. (D) Mn goes to +2 in acid; disproportionation involves one element.
Key point: MnO₄⁻ (acid) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺; 1 MnO₄⁻ ≡ 5 Fe²⁺; self-indicator.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Counting structural isomers of alkanes and of C₄H₁₀O, and classifying chain, position, functional and metamerism isomers
questions.question: Which set of counts and classifications is correct?
options: A) C₅H₁₂ has 2 isomers, C₆H₁₄ has 4, and C₄H₁₀O has 4
B) Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are functional isomers, and propanal and propanone are position isomers

C) C₄H₁₀ has 2, C₅H₁₂ has 3 and C₆H₁₄ has 5 structural isomers (chain isomers), so the number rises with carbon count; C₄H₁₀O has 7 (4 alcohols and 3 ethers); butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are position isomers, butan-1-ol and diethyl ether are functional isomers, diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether are metamers, and propanal and propanone are functional isomers
D) Metamerism occurs among alcohols that differ in the position of –OH
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2, 3, 5 alkane isomers; 7 for C₄H₁₀O; position, functional and metamer classifications as stated.
Concept: Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different properties are called isomers, and the phenomenon is called isomerism. Structural isomers differ in structure: when two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons, they are referred to as chain isomers (e.g. pentane, isopentane and neopentane for C₅H₁₂); when two or more compounds differ in the position of a substituent atom or functional group on the carbon skeleton, they are called position isomers (e.g. propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol); two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different functional groups are called functional isomers (e.g. propanone and propanal, or an alcohol and an ether); metamerism arises due to different alkyl chains on either side of the functional group in the molecule (e.g. C₄H₁₀O represents methoxypropane, CH₃OC₃H₇, and ethoxyethane, C₂H₅OC₂H₅). The alcohols of formula C₄H₁₀O are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (4), and the ethers are ethoxyethane, 1-methoxypropane and 2-methoxypropane (3).
Step 1: C₄H₁₀: butane, isobutane (2); C₅H₁₂: 3; C₆H₁₄: hexane, 2- and 3-methylpentane, 2,2- and 2,3-dimethylbutane (5).
Step 2: C₄H₁₀O: 4 alcohols + 3 ethers = 7.
Step 3: Classify each pair by what differs: position, functional group or alkyl groups around –O–.
Why: The number of ways to arrange carbons and place a functional group grows rapidly with molecular size.
Why not the others: (A) Undercounts every formula. (B) Classifications swapped. (D) Metamerism occurs in ethers, not in –OH position.
Key point: Alkanes C₄ 2, C₅ 3, C₆ 5; C₄H₁₀O 7; metamers differ in alkyl groups around a functional group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying an alkene from its ozonolysis products, calculating the masses of products, and comparing ozonolysis with oxidation by hot acidic KMnO₄
questions.question: An alkene C₅H₁₀ (M = 70 g mol⁻¹) on ozonolysis (O₃ then Zn/H₂O) gives ethanal and propanone. What is the alkene, what masses of ethanal (M = 44) and propanone (M = 58) are formed from 7.0 g at 100 % yield, and what does hot acidic KMnO₄ give instead?
options: A) Pent-2-ene; 4.4 g ethanal and 5.8 g propanone; KMnO₄ gives the same products

B) 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃; 4.4 g ethanal and 5.8 g propanone; hot acidic KMnO₄ cleaves the double bond and oxidises the CH₃CH= end to ethanoic acid, while the (CH₃)₂C= end remains propanone because it has no hydrogen on the doubly bonded carbon
C) 2-Methylbut-1-ene; 8.8 g ethanal; KMnO₄ gives butanoic acid
D) 2-Methylbut-2-ene; 2.2 g ethanal and 2.9 g propanone; KMnO₄ gives two carboxylic acids
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2-Methylbut-2-ene; 4.4 g ethanal, 5.8 g propanone; KMnO₄ gives ethanoic acid + propanone.
Concept: Ozonolysis of alkenes involves the addition of ozone molecule to the alkene to form an ozonide, and then cleavage of the ozonide by Zn-H₂O to smaller molecules; this reaction is highly useful in detecting the position of the double bond in alkenes or other unsaturated compounds; each doubly bonded carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon, so joining the carbonyl carbons of the products by a double bond reconstructs the alkene. Alkenes on reaction with acidic potassium permanganate or acidic potassium dichromate are oxidised to ketones and/or acids depending upon the nature of the alkene and the experimental conditions: a doubly bonded carbon carrying hydrogen (=CHR) becomes a carboxylic acid (=CH₂ becomes CO₂), while a doubly bonded carbon carrying two alkyl groups (=CR₂) becomes a ketone.
Given: C₅H₁₀, 7.0 g; products ethanal (CH₃CHO) and propanone ((CH₃)₂CO).
Formula/Principle: Join C=O carbons of products by C=C; 1 mol alkene → 1 mol of each carbonyl.
Step 1: CH₃CH=O + O=C(CH₃)₂ ⇒ CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂, 2-methylbut-2-ene.
Step 2: n = 7.0/70 = 0.10 mol.
Step 3: Ethanal = 0.10 × 44 = 4.4 g; propanone = 0.10 × 58 = 5.8 g.
Why: Ozonolysis stops at aldehydes with Zn/H₂O, whereas hot acidic permanganate oxidises aldehyde-forming ends further to acids.
Why not the others: (A) Pent-2-ene gives ethanal + propanal; KMnO₄ products differ. (C) That alkene gives methanal + butanone. (D) Masses halved; the =C(CH₃)₂ end gives a ketone.
Key point: Ozonolysis products locate C=C; KMnO₄: =CHR → acid, =CR₂ → ketone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading Henry's law constants at two temperatures to calculate the mole fraction of a dissolved gas, interpreting the graph of mole fraction against partial pressure, and applications of Henry's law
questions.question: For O₂ in water, K_H = 34.86 kbar at 293 K and 46.82 kbar at 303 K. A graph of mole fraction of dissolved O₂ against its partial pressure is a straight line through the origin. Which reading is correct?
options: A) At 293 K and p(O₂) = 0.20 bar, x(O₂) = 0.20/34 860 ≈ 5.7 × 10⁻⁶; the slope of the graph is 1/K_H; since K_H rises with temperature, O₂ is less soluble in warmer water, which is why aquatic animals are more comfortable in cold water; scuba divers face 'bends' when dissolved N₂ comes out of blood on rapid ascent, soft-drink bottles are sealed under high CO₂ pressure, and climbers at high altitude suffer anoxia due to low O₂ partial pressure
B) A higher K_H means higher solubility, so O₂ is more soluble at 303 K
C) The graph has slope K_H and does not pass through the origin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) x ≈ 5.7 × 10⁻⁶; slope 1/K_H; solubility falls with temperature; applications.
Concept: Henry's law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas present above the surface of liquid or solution; the most commonly used form of Henry's law states that the partial pressure of the gas in vapour phase (p) is proportional to the mole fraction of the gas (x) in the solution: p = K_H x, where K_H is the Henry's law constant. A plot of partial pressure of the gas against its mole fraction in solution is linear; equivalently, a plot of x against p is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/K_H. Different gases have different K_H values at the same temperature, so K_H is a function of the nature of the gas; the higher the value of K_H at a given pressure, the lower is the solubility of the gas in the liquid; K_H values for both N₂ and O₂ increase with increase of temperature, indicating that the solubility of gases increases with decrease of temperature; it is due to this reason that aquatic species are more comfortable in cold waters rather than in warm waters. Henry's law finds several applications: to increase the solubility of CO₂ in soft drinks and soda water, the bottle is sealed under high pressure; scuba divers breathing air at high pressure have increased amounts of dissolved gases in their blood, and when they come towards the surface the pressure gradually decreases, releasing dissolved gases and leading to the formation of bubbles of nitrogen in the blood, which blocks capillaries and creates a medical condition known as bends; at high altitudes the partial pressure of oxygen is less than that at ground level, leading to low concentrations of oxygen in the blood and tissues of people living at high altitudes or climbers, and low blood oxygen causes climbers to become weak and unable to think clearly — symptoms of a condition known as anoxia.
Given: K_H(293 K) = 34.86 kbar = 34 860 bar; p = 0.20 bar.
Formula/Principle: x = p/K_H.
Step 1: x = 0.20/34 860 = 5.7 × 10⁻⁶.
Step 2: Slope of x versus p = 1/K_H.
Step 3: K_H(303) > K_H(293) ⇒ lower solubility at 303 K.
Why: Dissolving a gas is usually exothermic, so heating drives gas out of solution, raising K_H.
Why not the others: (B) Higher K_H means lower solubility. (C) Slope is 1/K_H and the line passes through the origin. (D) Mole fraction cannot exceed 1; divide, not multiply.
Key point: p = K_H x; higher K_H ⇒ lower solubility; K_H increases with T.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing masses deposited by the same charge in different electrolytic cells using Faraday's laws, and explaining products of electrolysis of aqueous NaCl
questions.question: The same charge of 1 F (96 500 C) is passed through cells containing molten AlCl₃, aqueous CuSO₄ and aqueous AgNO₃ (inert electrodes). What masses of Al, Cu and Ag are deposited (atomic masses 27, 63.5, 108), what charge deposits 1.08 g of Ag, and what forms at the electrodes when aqueous NaCl is electrolysed?
options: A) 27 g, 63.5 g, 108 g; 96 500 C; Na at the cathode
B) 9.0 g, 63.5 g, 108 g; 965 C; O₂ at the anode only
C) 9.0 g, 31.75 g, 54 g; 9650 C; Na and Cl₂

D) Al 9.0 g (1/3 mol), Cu 31.75 g (1/2 mol), Ag 108 g (1 mol), so mass deposited Ag > Cu > Al; 965 C deposits 1.08 g Ag; in aqueous NaCl, H₂ is liberated at the cathode (water is reduced in preference to Na⁺) and Cl₂ at the anode (because of the overpotential for O₂ evolution), leaving NaOH in solution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Al 9.0 g, Cu 31.75 g, Ag 108 g; 965 C; H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode.
Concept: Faraday's first law states that the amount of chemical reaction which occurs at any electrode during electrolysis by a current is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte (solution or melt); the second law states that the amounts of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity passing through the electrolytic solution are proportional to their chemical equivalent weights (atomic mass of metal ÷ number of electrons required to reduce the cation). The charge on one mole of electrons is approximately 96 500 C mol⁻¹, called the Faraday constant F. For Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, one mole of electrons is required; for Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, two moles; for Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, three moles. Products of electrolysis depend on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrodes; in aqueous NaCl, at the cathode there is competition between Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (E° = −2.71 V) and H₂O + e⁻ → ½H₂ + OH⁻ (E° = −0.83 V); the reaction with higher E° is preferred, so H₂ is evolved; at the anode, although O₂ evolution has a lower E°, chlorine is liberated because of the overpotential of oxygen; the net reaction gives NaOH, H₂ and Cl₂.
Given: Q = 96 500 C = 1 F; n electrons: Al 3, Cu 2, Ag 1.
Formula/Principle: Moles deposited = Q/(nF); mass = moles × atomic mass.
Step 1: Al: 1/3 × 27 = 9.0 g; Cu: 1/2 × 63.5 = 31.75 g; Ag: 1 × 108 = 108 g.
Step 2: 1.08 g Ag = 0.010 mol ⇒ Q = 0.010 × 96 500 = 965 C.
Step 3: Aqueous NaCl: water reduced at cathode (H₂); Cl⁻ oxidised at anode (Cl₂).
Why: Each ion needs as many electrons as its charge, so one faraday deposits one mole of electrons' worth of metal, divided by ionic charge.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores ionic charges; Na cannot form in water. (B) Cu needs 2 e⁻; Cl₂ forms at the anode. (C) Ag needs 1 e⁻; charge for 1.08 g is 965 C.
Key point: m = (Q/nF) × M; aqueous NaCl → H₂ (cathode), Cl₂ (anode).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the integrated rate equation, half-life and units for a zero-order reaction, and why reactions on a saturated catalyst surface are zero order
questions.question: Which explanation of zero-order reactions is correct?
options: A) The rate is proportional to the square of the concentration, and the half-life is constant
B) Zero-order reactions never reach completion because the rate is zero

C) For a zero-order reaction the rate is independent of concentration, so [R] = [R]₀ − kt, a plot of [R] against t is a straight line with slope −k, k has units mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, and t½ = [R]₀/2k, so the half-life is proportional to the initial concentration; the decomposition of NH₃ on a hot platinum surface at high pressure is zero order because the metal surface is saturated with gas molecules, so further increase in concentration cannot change the amount of NH₃ reacting per unit time
D) Zero-order reactions have k in s⁻¹ and t½ = 0.693/k
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) [R] = [R]₀ − kt; slope −k; units mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; t½ = [R]₀/2k; saturated surface explanation.
Concept: Zero order reaction means that the rate of the reaction is proportional to zero power of the concentration of reactants; for R → P, rate = −d[R]/dt = k[R]⁰ = k; integrating gives [R] = −kt + I, and at t = 0, [R] = [R]₀, so [R] = [R]₀ − kt; comparing with the equation of a straight line y = mx + c, if we plot [R] against t, we get a straight line with slope = −k and intercept equal to [R]₀; the units of k for a zero-order reaction are mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. The half-life of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to one half of its initial concentration; for a zero-order reaction, t½ = [R]₀/2k, so the half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration of the reactants. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions; some enzyme catalysed reactions and reactions which occur on metal surfaces are a few examples; the decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface is a zero order reaction at high pressure: 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) (1130 K, Pt catalyst); in this reaction, the platinum metal acts as a catalyst; at high pressure, the metal surface gets saturated with gas molecules, so a further change in reaction conditions is unable to alter the amount of ammonia on the surface of the catalyst, making the rate of the reaction independent of its concentration; the thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is another example.
Why: When every active site is already occupied, adding more reactant cannot increase the number reacting at once, so the rate stays constant.
Why not the others: (A) That is second order; zero-order t½ depends on [R]₀. (B) The rate is constant, not zero, until the reactant is used up. (D) Those are first-order expressions.
Key point: Zero order: [R] = [R]₀ − kt; t½ = [R]₀/2k; saturated surface.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Arranging 3d ions in order of spin-only magnetic moment and explaining their colour or lack of colour in terms of d–d transitions
questions.question: Which order of spin-only magnetic moment and explanation is correct for Ti³⁺, Cr³⁺, Mn²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺?
options: A) Mn²⁺ (3d⁵, 5 unpaired, 5.92 BM) > Cr³⁺ (3d³, 3.87 BM) > Ti³⁺ (3d¹) = Cu²⁺ (3d⁹), each 1.73 BM > Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰, 0); μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM where n is the number of unpaired electrons; ions with partly filled d orbitals are usually coloured because an electron absorbs visible light to jump between split d levels (d–d transition) and the complementary colour is seen, while Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) and Sc³⁺ (d⁰) are colourless
B) Zn²⁺ > Cu²⁺ > Mn²⁺, because magnetic moment increases with atomic number
C) All five ions have the same magnetic moment because they are transition-metal ions
D) Mn²⁺ is colourless because it has five unpaired electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mn²⁺ > Cr³⁺ > Ti³⁺ = Cu²⁺ > Zn²⁺; μ = √(n(n + 2)); colour from d–d transitions, d⁰/d¹⁰ colourless.
Concept: When a magnetic field is applied to substances, mainly two types of magnetic behaviour are observed: diamagnetism and paramagnetism; diamagnetic substances are repelled by the applied field while paramagnetic substances are attracted; paramagnetism arises from the presence of unpaired electrons, each such electron having a magnetic moment associated with its spin angular momentum and orbital angular momentum; for the compounds of the first series of transition metals, the contribution of the orbital angular momentum is effectively quenched and hence is of no significance; for these, the magnetic moment is determined by the number of unpaired electrons and is calculated by using the 'spin-only' formula μ = √(n(n + 2)), where n is the number of unpaired electrons and μ is the magnetic moment in units of Bohr magneton (BM); a single unpaired electron has a magnetic moment of 1.73 Bohr magnetons. When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed; this frequency generally lies in the visible region; the colour observed corresponds to the complementary colour of the light absorbed; the frequency of the light absorbed is determined by the nature of the ligand; ions with no d electrons (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) or completely filled d subshells (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) cannot undergo d–d transitions and are colourless.
Given: Ti³⁺ 3d¹, Cr³⁺ 3d³, Mn²⁺ 3d⁵, Cu²⁺ 3d⁹, Zn²⁺ 3d¹⁰.
Formula/Principle: μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM.
Step 1: Unpaired n: Ti³⁺ 1, Cr³⁺ 3, Mn²⁺ 5, Cu²⁺ 1, Zn²⁺ 0.
Step 2: μ: 1.73, 3.87, 5.92, 1.73, 0.
Step 3: Order Mn²⁺ > Cr³⁺ > Ti³⁺ = Cu²⁺ > Zn²⁺.
Why: The moment depends only on the number of unpaired electrons, which peaks at d⁵ and is equal for d¹ and d⁹.
Why not the others: (B) Moment follows unpaired electrons, not atomic number. (C) Unpaired counts differ. (D) Mn²⁺ salts are pale pink; it is not d⁰ or d¹⁰.
Key point: μ = √(n(n + 2)); d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions are colourless and diamagnetic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading data on chromium(III) chloride hydrates — colour and moles of AgCl precipitated — to identify hydrate isomers, and recognising coordination and linkage isomerism
questions.question:
Three compounds with formula CrCl₃·6H₂O are each treated with excess AgNO₃.

Compound | Colour | mol AgCl per mol
X | violet | 3
Y | grey-green | 2
Z | dark green | 1

Which reading of the data is correct?
options: A) X, Y and Z are geometrical isomers of [Cr(H₂O)₃Cl₃]
B) All three contain six coordinated chloride ions
C) X is [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O and Z is [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃

D) X is [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃, Y is [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O and Z is [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O; they are solvate (hydrate) isomers, differing in whether water is a ligand or lattice water; other structural isomers include coordination isomers such as [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆], and linkage isomers in which an ambidentate ligand like NO₂⁻ binds through N (nitrito-N) or O (nitrito-O)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) X [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃, Y [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O, Z [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O; hydrate isomers; coordination and linkage isomerism.
Concept: Structural isomers arise due to differences in bonding between the ligands and the central atom. Solvate isomerism is a form known as 'hydrate isomerism' in case water is involved as a solvent; this is similar to ionisation isomerism; solvate isomers differ by whether or not a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal ion or merely present as free solvent molecules in the crystal lattice; an example is provided by the aqua complex [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet) and its solvate isomer [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (grey-green). Only the chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are precipitated as AgCl. Coordination isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex, e.g. [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆], in which the NH₃ ligands are bound to Co³⁺ and the CN⁻ ligands to Cr³⁺, and in its coordination isomer [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆] the NH₃ ligands are bound to Cr³⁺ and the CN⁻ ligands to Co³⁺. Linkage isomerism arises in a coordination compound containing an ambidentate ligand; a simple example is provided by complexes containing the thiocyanate ligand, NCS⁻, which may bind through the nitrogen to give M–NCS or through sulphur to give M–SCN; similarly NO₂⁻ can bind through N or O.
Given: AgCl per mole: 3, 2, 1.
Formula/Principle: Precipitated Cl⁻ = counter ions; coordination number of Cr³⁺ = 6.
Step 1: X: 3 free Cl⁻ ⇒ six H₂O ligands.
Step 2: Y: 2 free Cl⁻ ⇒ one Cl⁻ and five H₂O ligands, one lattice H₂O.
Step 3: Z: 1 free Cl⁻ ⇒ two Cl⁻ and four H₂O ligands, two lattice H₂O.
Why: Exchanging a coordinated water for a chloride changes how many chlorides are free, and also changes colour because the ligand set changes.
Why not the others: (A) Different numbers of free Cl⁻ show different compositions of the coordination sphere. (B) Only Z has two coordinated Cl⁻ at most. (C) X and Z swapped.
Key point: Hydrate isomers differ in coordinated versus lattice water; AgCl counts free Cl⁻.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking the geometry of complexes to geometrical and optical isomerism in square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], octahedral [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ and [Co(en)₃]³⁺, and tetrahedral complexes
questions.question: Which statement about stereoisomerism in complexes is correct?
options: A) Tetrahedral [MA₂B₂] complexes show cis and trans isomers

B) Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] exists as cis and trans isomers (the cis isomer, cisplatin, is used against cancer); [Co(en)₃]³⁺ exists as two non-superimposable mirror images (optical isomers, d and l); cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ is optically active while the trans isomer is not, because the trans form has a plane of symmetry; tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because all positions are adjacent
C) trans-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ is optically active because it contains chelating ligands
D) [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows optical isomerism but not geometrical isomerism
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂ cis/trans; [Co(en)₃]³⁺ optical; cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ optically active, trans not; no geometrical isomers for tetrahedral.
Concept: Geometrical isomerism arises in heteroleptic complexes due to different possible geometric arrangements of the ligands; important examples of this behaviour are found with coordination numbers 4 and 6; in a square planar complex of formula [MX₂L₂] (X and L are unidentate), the two ligands X may be arranged adjacent to each other in a cis isomer, or opposite to each other in a trans isomer, as in [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]; geometrical isomerism is not possible for tetrahedral complexes as the relative positions of the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom are the same with respect to each other. Octahedral complexes of formula [MX₂(L–L)₂], where L–L is a bidentate ligand (e.g. NH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂, en), also show cis and trans isomerism. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another; the molecules or ions that cannot be superimposed are called chiral; the two forms are called dextro (d) and laevo (l) depending upon the direction they rotate the plane of polarised light in a polarimeter; optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands, e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺; in a coordination entity of the type [PtCl₂(en)₂]²⁺ or [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺, only the cis-isomer shows optical activity. cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin) is used in the treatment of cancer.
Why: Optical activity needs the absence of a mirror plane, while geometrical isomerism needs positions that can be either adjacent or opposite.
Why not the others: (A) In a tetrahedron all positions are adjacent. (C) The trans isomer has a mirror plane. (D) The square planar complex has a mirror plane but cis/trans forms.
Key point: Square planar MA₂B₂: cis/trans; octahedral with en: cis optically active; tetrahedral: no geometrical isomers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking the uses of dichloromethane, chloroform, iodoform, carbon tetrachloride, freons and DDT to their health and environmental effects
questions.question: Which statement about polyhalogen compounds is correct?
options: A) Chloroform is stored in clear, open bottles because it is stable in air and light
B) DDT is readily biodegraded, so it does not accumulate in animals

C) Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light to the very poisonous phosgene (COCl₂), so it is stored in closed dark-coloured bottles filled to the brim; iodoform's antiseptic action is due to liberation of free iodine; dichloromethane, used as a solvent and paint remover, harms the central nervous system; carbon tetrachloride and freons (chlorofluorocarbons) released into the air reach the stratosphere and deplete the ozone layer; DDT, an insecticide, is not metabolised rapidly by animals and is deposited and stored in fatty tissues
D) Freons are toxic gases that react quickly in the lower atmosphere
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chloroform → phosgene (stored dark, full); iodoform releases I₂; CH₂Cl₂ affects CNS; CCl₄ and freons deplete ozone; DDT accumulates in fat.
Concept: Dichloromethane is widely used as a solvent, as a paint remover, as a propellant in aerosols, and as a process solvent in the manufacture of drugs; methylene chloride harms the human central nervous system; exposure to lower levels of methylene chloride in air can lead to slightly impaired hearing and vision. Chemically, chloroform is employed as a solvent for fats, alkaloids, iodine and other substances; the major use of chloroform today is in the production of the freon refrigerant R-22; it was once used as a general anaesthetic in surgery but has been replaced by less toxic, safer anaesthetics, such as ether; chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light to an extremely poisonous gas, carbonyl chloride, also known as phosgene; it is therefore stored in closed dark coloured bottles completely filled so that air is kept out. Iodoform was used earlier as an antiseptic, but the antiseptic properties are due to the liberation of free iodine and not due to iodoform itself; due to its objectionable smell, it has been replaced by other formulations containing iodine. Carbon tetrachloride is used in the manufacture of refrigerants and propellants for aerosol cans; when carbon tetrachloride is released into air, it rises to the atmosphere and depletes the ozone layer. The chlorofluorocarbon compounds of methane and ethane are collectively known as freons; they are extremely stable, unreactive, non-toxic, non-corrosive and easily liquefiable gases; most freon, even that used in refrigeration, eventually makes its way into the atmosphere where it diffuses unchanged into the stratosphere; in the stratosphere, freon is able to initiate radical chain reactions that can upset the natural ozone balance. DDT, the first chlorinated organic insecticide, is not metabolised very rapidly by animals; instead, it is deposited and stored in the fatty tissues; if ingestion continues at a steady rate, DDT builds up within the animal over time.
Why: The stability or reactivity of each compound decides both its usefulness and its harm — unreactive freons survive to reach the ozone layer, and fat-soluble DDT accumulates.
Why not the others: (A) Light and air convert chloroform to phosgene. (B) DDT persists and accumulates. (D) Freons are non-toxic and unreactive, which is why they reach the stratosphere.
Key point: CHCl₃ → COCl₂ (store dark, full); freons and CCl₄ deplete ozone; DDT accumulates.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the choice of reactants in Williamson ether synthesis and the products and mechanisms of cleavage of methyl tert-butyl ether and anisole by HI
questions.question: Which explanation about the preparation and cleavage of ethers is correct?
options: A) To make tert-butyl methyl ether by Williamson synthesis, sodium tert-butoxide is treated with methyl bromide, because the reaction is SN2 and needs an unhindered primary halide, whereas tert-butyl bromide with sodium methoxide gives mainly 2-methylpropene by elimination; with HI, methyl tert-butyl ether gives methanol and tert-butyl iodide because cleavage proceeds through the stable tert-butyl carbocation (SN1); anisole with HI gives phenol and methyl iodide, because the O–aryl bond is strengthened by partial double-bond character and the phenyl cation is unstable
B) Tert-butyl bromide with sodium methoxide is the best route to tert-butyl methyl ether
C) Anisole with HI gives iodobenzene and methanol
D) Methyl tert-butyl ether with HI always gives methyl iodide and tert-butyl alcohol by SN2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Williamson: tert-butoxide + CH₃Br; MTBE + HI → CH₃OH + (CH₃)₃CI (SN1); anisole + HI → phenol + CH₃I.
Concept: Williamson synthesis is an important laboratory method for the preparation of symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers; in this method, an alkyl halide is allowed to react with sodium alkoxide; ethers containing substituted alkyl groups (secondary or tertiary) may also be prepared by this method; the reaction involves SN2 attack of an alkoxide ion on a primary alkyl halide; better results are obtained if the alkyl halide is primary; in case of secondary and tertiary alkyl halides, elimination competes over substitution; if a tertiary alkyl halide is used, an alkene is the only reaction product and no ether is formed, e.g. the reaction of CH₃ONa with (CH₃)₃C–Br gives exclusively 2-methylpropene; this is because alkoxides are not only nucleophiles but strong bases as well. Ethers are the least reactive of the functional groups; the cleavage of the C–O bond in ethers takes place under drastic conditions with excess of hydrogen halides; the order of reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI > HBr > HCl. When primary or secondary alkyl groups are present, it is the lower alkyl group that forms alkyl iodide (SN2 reaction); when one of the alkyl groups is a tertiary group, the halide formed is a tertiary halide: (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₃ + HI → CH₃OH + (CH₃)₃C–I; it is because in step 2 of the reaction the departure of the leaving group (HO–CH₃) creates a more stable carbocation [(CH₃)₃C⁺], and the reaction follows the SN1 mechanism. In case of anisole, methylphenyl oxonium ion is formed by protonation of ether; the bond between O–CH₃ is weaker than the bond between O–C₆H₅ because the carbon of the phenyl group is sp² hybridised and there is a partial double bond character; therefore the attack by I⁻ ion breaks the O–CH₃ bond to form CH₃I; phenols do not react further to give halides because the sp² hybridised carbon of phenol cannot undergo nucleophilic substitution reaction needed for conversion to the halide.
Why: Mechanism decides the outcome: SN2 needs an unhindered carbon, SN1 needs a stable carbocation, and neither can occur at an aryl carbon.
Why not the others: (B) This gives an alkene by elimination. (C) The O–aryl bond is not cleaved. (D) The tert-butyl group leaves as a carbocation (SN1).
Key point: Williamson: alkoxide + primary halide; HI cleavage: tertiary → SN1; aryl–O bond stays intact.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering acid derivatives by reactivity towards nucleophilic acyl substitution, and naming preparations and reactions of carboxylic acids
questions.question: Which order and set of facts is correct?
options: A) Amides > esters > anhydrides > acid chlorides in reactivity towards nucleophiles
B) Carboxylic acids undergo α-halogenation without any catalyst, and soda lime adds a carbon atom

C) Reactivity towards nucleophilic acyl substitution: acyl chloride > acid anhydride > ester > amide, because a better leaving group (Cl⁻ is the weakest base) and less resonance donation into the C=O make the carbonyl carbon more reactive; carboxylic acids are prepared by oxidising primary alcohols or aldehydes, by oxidising alkylbenzenes with alkaline KMnO₄ (toluene → benzoic acid), and by hydrolysing nitriles; with Cl₂ or Br₂ and a little red phosphorus, acids with α-hydrogens give α-halo acids (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction), and heating the sodium salt with soda lime removes CO₂ to give an alkane with one carbon less
D) Toluene is oxidised by KMnO₄ to benzyl alcohol only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide; preparations; HVZ; decarboxylation with soda lime.
Concept: Acid derivatives react with nucleophiles by addition to the carbonyl followed by elimination of the leaving group; the more stable (weaker base) the leaving group and the less the lone pair on the attached atom donates into the carbonyl by resonance, the more reactive the derivative; Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group and chlorine donates little, so acyl chlorides are most reactive; in amides the nitrogen lone pair is strongly delocalised into C=O, so amides are least reactive. Primary alcohols are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids with common oxidising agents such as potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) in neutral, acidic or alkaline media or by potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) and chromium trioxide (CrO₃) in acidic media; aromatic carboxylic acids can be prepared by vigorous oxidation of alkylbenzenes with chromic acid or acidic or alkaline potassium permanganate — the entire side chain is oxidised to the carboxyl group irrespective of length of the side chain; nitriles are hydrolysed to amides and then to acids in the presence of H⁺ or OH⁻ as catalyst. Carboxylic acids having an α-hydrogen are halogenated at the α-position on treatment with chlorine or bromine in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus to give α-halocarboxylic acids; the reaction is known as the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction. Carboxylic acids lose carbon dioxide to form hydrocarbons when their sodium salts are heated with sodalime (NaOH and CaO in the ratio of 3 : 1); the reaction is known as decarboxylation.
Why: The ability of the substituent to leave and its electron donation into the carbonyl together control how readily nucleophiles attack.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (B) HVZ needs red phosphorus; soda lime removes a carbon. (D) The side chain is oxidised fully to –COOH.
Key point: RCOCl > (RCO)₂O > RCOOR′ > RCONH₂; HVZ; soda lime decarboxylation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating reagent and product masses and gas volume in preparing benzenediazonium chloride from aniline and converting it to iodobenzene, phenol and an azo dye
questions.question: 9.3 g of aniline (M = 93 g mol⁻¹) is diazotised with NaNO₂ (M = 69) and HCl at 273–278 K. What mass of NaNO₂ is needed, what mass of iodobenzene (M = 204) forms with KI at 70 % yield, what volume of N₂ (at STP, 22.7 L mol⁻¹) would be released if the whole diazonium salt were instead warmed with water, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 69 g NaNO₂; 20.4 g iodobenzene; 22.7 L N₂
B) 6.9 g NaNO₂; 20.4 g iodobenzene; 1.14 L N₂; diazonium salts are stable at room temperature
C) 3.45 g NaNO₂; 14.3 g iodobenzene; 4.54 L N₂; diazotisation needs a high temperature

D) 6.9 g NaNO₂ (0.10 mol); 0.10 × 0.70 × 204 ≈ 14.3 g iodobenzene; 0.10 × 22.7 = 2.27 L N₂ while phenol forms; the reaction is kept at 273–278 K because arenediazonium salts decompose on warming, and coupling of the diazonium ion with phenol in alkaline medium gives orange p-hydroxyazobenzene, an azo dye, through electrophilic substitution at the para position
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6.9 g NaNO₂; 14.3 g iodobenzene; 2.27 L N₂; low temperature needed; azo coupling.
Concept: Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared by the reaction of aniline with nitrous acid at 273–278 K; nitrous acid is produced in the reaction mixture by the reaction of sodium nitrite with hydrochloric acid; the conversion of primary aromatic amines into diazonium salts is known as diazotisation; due to its instability, the diazonium salt is not generally stored and is used immediately after its preparation. Iodine is not easy to introduce into the benzene ring directly, but when the diazonium salt solution is treated with potassium iodide, iodobenzene is formed. If the temperature of the diazonium salt solution is allowed to rise up to 283 K, the salt gets hydrolysed to phenol with evolution of N₂. Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with phenol in which the phenol molecule at its para position is coupled with the diazonium salt to form p-hydroxyazobenzene; this type of reaction is known as a coupling reaction; the azo products obtained have an extended conjugate system having both the aromatic rings joined through the –N=N– bond; these compounds are often coloured and are used as dyes; benzene diazonium chloride reacts with phenol in alkaline medium to give an orange dye.
Given: 9.3 g aniline (M 93); NaNO₂ M 69; iodobenzene M 204; 70 % yield; 22.7 L mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: 1 mol C₆H₅NH₂ → 1 mol C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ → 1 mol C₆H₅I or 1 mol C₆H₅OH + 1 mol N₂.
Step 1: n = 9.3/93 = 0.10 mol ⇒ NaNO₂ = 0.10 × 69 = 6.9 g.
Step 2: Iodobenzene = 0.10 × 0.70 × 204 = 14.3 g.
Step 3: N₂ = 0.10 × 22.7 = 2.27 L.
Why: Each aniline molecule forms one diazonium ion, which can lose one N₂ when it reacts, so moles carry through each step.
Why not the others: (A) Moles multiplied by 10; yield ignored. (B) Yield ignored; N₂ halved; salts are unstable. (C) Half the NaNO₂; N₂ doubled; low temperature is needed.
Key point: ArNH₂ → ArN₂⁺ (273–278 K) → ArI (KI), ArOH + N₂ (warm), azo dye (phenol).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Relating the structure and chemical nature of enzymes, hormones, vitamins and nucleic acids to their functions and deficiency effects
questions.question: Which statement about biomolecules is correct?
options: A) All hormones are proteins, and vitamin C is fat-soluble

B) Most enzymes are globular proteins that catalyse specific reactions by lowering activation energy; hormones may be polypeptides (insulin), amino acid derivatives (thyroxine, adrenaline) or steroids (oestrogens, androgens); vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and stored in liver and adipose tissue, while B-group vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble and must be supplied regularly (except vitamin B₁₂); vitamin D deficiency causes rickets and vitamin K deficiency increases blood clotting time; DNA contains 2-deoxy-D-ribose and thymine and is double-stranded, while RNA contains D-ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded
C) DNA contains uracil, and RNA is a double helix
D) Enzymes are carbohydrates that are consumed in the reactions they catalyse
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Enzymes are globular proteins; hormone classes; fat- and water-soluble vitamins with deficiencies; DNA vs RNA.
Concept: Almost all the enzymes are globular proteins; enzymes are very specific for a particular reaction and for a particular substrate; they are generally named after the compound or class of compounds upon which they work; enzymes catalyse reactions by reducing the magnitude of the energy barrier (activation energy) and are not consumed. Hormones are molecules that act as intercellular messengers; these are produced by endocrine glands in the body and are poured directly into the blood stream which transports them to the site of action; in terms of chemical nature, some of these are steroids, e.g. estrogens and androgens; some are polypeptides, for example insulin and endorphins; and some others are amino acid derivatives such as epinephrine and norepinephrine (and thyroxine). Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat: fat soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E and K) are soluble in fat and oils but insoluble in water; they are stored in liver and adipose (fat storing) tissues; water soluble vitamins (B group vitamins and vitamin C) must be supplied regularly in diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin B₁₂) in our body; deficiency of vitamin D causes rickets (bone deformities in children) and osteomalacia (soft bones and joint pain in adults); deficiency of vitamin K increases blood clotting time. The sugar moiety in DNA molecules is β-D-2-deoxyribose whereas in RNA molecule it is β-D-ribose; DNA contains four bases viz. adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T); RNA also contains four bases, the first three bases are the same as in DNA but the fourth is uracil (U); DNA has a double-strand helix structure while RNA molecules are of three types and contain a single strand of the helix (which sometimes folds back on itself).
Why: The chemical class of each biomolecule determines how it is stored, transported and used in the body.
Why not the others: (A) Hormones include steroids and amino acid derivatives; vitamin C is water-soluble. (C) Bases and strandedness swapped. (D) Enzymes are proteins and are not consumed.
Key point: Fat-soluble A, D, E, K; water-soluble B, C; DNA deoxyribose + T, RNA ribose + U.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Classifying real functions as one-one, onto, both or neither using the horizontal line test on their graphs
questions.question: Consider \(f_1(x)=x^3,\ f_2(x)=x^3-x,\ f_3(x)=e^x,\ f_4(x)=2x+3\), each from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R\). How many are bijective, which is onto but not one-one, and which is one-one but not onto?
options: A) \(4;\ \text{none};\ \text{none}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2\ (f_1,f_4);\ f_2\text{ onto, not one-one};\ f_3\text{ one-one, not onto}\)
Given: \(f_1=x^3,\ f_2=x^3-x,\ f_3=e^x,\ f_4=2x+3\text{ on }\mathbb R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{one-one: every horizontal line meets the graph at most once; onto: every horizontal line meets it at least once}\)
Step 1: \(f_1,f_4\text{ strictly increasing and unbounded both ways}\Rightarrow\text{bijective}\)
Step 2: \(f_2(-1)=f_2(0)=f_2(1)=0\Rightarrow\text{not one-one};\ \text{continuous, unbounded both ways}\Rightarrow\text{onto}\)
Step 3: \(f_3\text{ strictly increasing}\Rightarrow\text{one-one};\ e^x>0\Rightarrow\text{range }(0,\infty)\ne\mathbb R\)
Worked derivation: \[f_4(x)=y\Rightarrow x=\frac{y-3}{2}\in\mathbb R\ \text{for every }y\]
Check: \[y=0\text{ meets }y=x^3-x\text{ three times; }y=-1\text{ never meets }y=e^x\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the horizontal line test reads injectivity and surjectivity directly off the graph}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f_2,f_3\text{ fail}\); (B) \(f_1\text{ is bijective; }f_2\text{ is not one-one}\); (C) \(f_3\text{ is not onto}\).
Key point: \(\text{strictly monotonic + full range}\Rightarrow\text{bijective}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving the Cauchy functional equation f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) at integers and counting all, onto and one-one functions between finite sets
questions.question: If \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\) for all real \(x,y\) and \(f(1)=3\), what is \(f(5)\)? For \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) and \(B=\{a,b\}\), how many functions \(A\to B\) are there, how many are onto, and how many one-one functions \(B\to A\) are there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(15;\ 8;\ 6;\ 6\)
Given: \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),\ f(1)=3;\ |A|=3,\ |B|=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(f(n)=nf(1)\text{ for integers }n;\ \#(A\to B)=|B|^{|A|};\ \text{onto}=\text{total}-\text{non-onto}\)
Step 1: \(f(2)=f(1)+f(1)=6,\ \ldots,\ f(5)=5f(1)=15\)
Step 2: \(\text{all functions}=2^3=8;\ \text{non-onto}=2\ (\text{constant})\Rightarrow\text{onto}=6\)
Step 3: \(\text{one-one }B\to A:\ 3\times2=6\)
Worked derivation: \[f(0)=f(0+0)=2f(0)\Rightarrow f(0)=0;\ f(n+1)=f(n)+3\Rightarrow f(n)=3n\]
Check: \[f(2+3)=6+9=15\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{additivity turns the function into repeated addition of }f(1)\text{; counting assigns an image to each element}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{treats }f\text{ as multiplicative; counts }3^2\); (C) \(\text{wrong counts}\); (D) \(\text{wrong }f(5)\text{ and counts}\).
Key point: \(|B|^{|A|}\text{ functions};\ \text{onto from 3 to 2 elements}=2^3-2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reducing a trigonometric equation to a quadratic in sin x, writing its general solution and counting solutions in given intervals
questions.question: For \(2\cos^2x+3\sin x=0\), what is the general solution, and how many solutions lie in \([0,2\pi]\) and in \([0,4\pi]\)?
options: B) \(x=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6;\ 4;\ 8\)
D) \(x=n\pi-\dfrac\pi6;\ 1;\ 2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(x=n\pi+(-1)^{n+1}\dfrac\pi6;\ 2;\ 4\)
Given: \(2\cos^2x+3\sin x=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin x=\sin\alpha\Rightarrow x=n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha\)
Step 1: \(2-2\sin^2x+3\sin x=0\Rightarrow2\sin^2x-3\sin x-2=0\Rightarrow(2\sin x+1)(\sin x-2)=0\)
Step 2: \(\sin x=2\text{ impossible};\ \sin x=-\tfrac12=\sin\left(-\tfrac\pi6\right)\Rightarrow x=n\pi+(-1)^n\left(-\tfrac\pi6\right)\)
Step 3: \([0,2\pi]:\ \tfrac{7\pi}6,\tfrac{11\pi}6\ (2);\ [0,4\pi]:\ \text{add }2\pi\text{ to each}\ (4)\)
Worked derivation: \[n=1:\ \pi+\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac{7\pi}6;\ n=2:\ 2\pi-\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac{11\pi}6\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac{7\pi}6:\ 2\cdot\tfrac34+3\left(-\tfrac12\right)=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{writing everything in }\sin x\text{ gives a quadratic; only roots in }[-1,1]\text{ give solutions}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives }\sin x=+\tfrac12\); (B) \(\text{uses the cosine form}\); (D) \(\text{misses half the solutions}\).
Key point: \(|\sin x|\le1\text{ rejects the root }2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding integer values of a coefficient for which a monic quadratic has integer roots, and using conjugate surds as roots of a quadratic with rational coefficients
questions.question: For how many integers \(k\) does \(x^2-kx+12=0\) have integer roots? If \(2+\sqrt3\) is a root of \(x^2+bx+c=0\) with rational \(b,c\), what are \(b\) and \(c\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(6;\ b=-4,\ c=1\)
Given: \(x^2-kx+12=0;\ \text{root }2+\sqrt3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\alpha+\beta=k,\ \alpha\beta=12;\ \text{rational coefficients}\Rightarrow\text{irrational roots in conjugate pairs}\)
Step 1: \(\text{integer pairs with product }12:\ (1,12),(2,6),(3,4)\text{ and their negatives}\)
Step 2: \(k=\pm13,\pm8,\pm7\Rightarrow6\text{ values}\)
Step 3: \(\text{roots }2\pm\sqrt3:\ \text{sum }4,\ \text{product }1\Rightarrow b=-4,\ c=1\)
Worked derivation: \[(x-2-\sqrt3)(x-2+\sqrt3)=(x-2)^2-3=x^2-4x+1\]
Check: \[k=7:\ x^2-7x+12=(x-3)(x-4)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a monic integer quadratic has integer roots exactly when they split the constant term; conjugates make the coefficients rational}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ignores negative pairs; sign of }b\text{ wrong}\); (C) \(c\text{ is the product }1\); (D) \(\text{counts ordered pairs; }c\text{ must be rational}\).
Key point: \(\text{rational coefficients}\Rightarrow p+\sqrt q\text{ and }p-\sqrt q\text{ together}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the fundamental principle of counting to four-digit numbers with distinct digits, even ones, and three-digit multiples of 5 with distinct digits
questions.question: How many four-digit numbers have distinct digits, how many of these are even, and how many three-digit numbers with distinct digits are divisible by \(5\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(4536;\ 2296;\ 136\)
Given: \(\text{digits }0\text{–}9;\ \text{first digit non-zero};\ \text{digits distinct}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{multiply the number of choices for each place, filling restricted places first}\)
Step 1: \(\text{four-digit: }9\times9\times8\times7=4536\)
Step 2: \(\text{even, last }0:\ 9\times8\times7=504;\ \text{last }2,4,6,8:\ 4\times8\times8\times7=1792;\ \text{total }2296\)
Step 3: \(\text{three-digit, last }0:\ 9\times8=72;\ \text{last }5:\ 8\times8=64;\ \text{total }136\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{last digit }e\in\{2,4,6,8\}:\ \text{first digit }\ne0,e\ (8),\ \text{then }8,\ 7\]
Check: \[504+1792=2296\ne\tfrac12(4536)\text{ because }0\text{ is an even digit}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the zero restriction on the first digit interacts with the last-digit condition, so cases must be split}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{allows a leading zero}\); (B) \(\text{assumes exactly half are even}\); (D) \(\text{ignores distinctness}\).
Key point: \(\text{split cases when }0\text{ affects both a restricted place and the condition}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the sum of n terms of a G.P. to find when partial sums first exceed a value, and the sum of an infinite G.P. with |r| < 1
questions.question: For the G.P. \(3,6,12,\ldots\), what is the least \(n\) for which \(S_n>1000\), and what is \(S_n\) then? What is the sum of the infinite G.P. \(1+\tfrac13+\tfrac19+\cdots\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(n=9,\ S_9=1533;\ \tfrac32\)
Given: \(a=3,\ r=2;\ a'=1,\ r'=\tfrac13\)
Formula/Principle: \(S_n=\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1};\ S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}\ (|r|<1)\)
Step 1: \(S_n=3(2^n-1)>1000\Rightarrow2^n>334.3\)
Step 2: \(2^8=256<334.3<512=2^9\Rightarrow n=9\)
Step 3: \(S_9=3(511)=1533;\ S_\infty=\dfrac{1}{1-\frac13}=\dfrac32\)
Worked derivation: \[S_8=3(255)=765<1000<1533=S_9\]
Check: \[T_9=3\cdot2^8=768,\ S_8+T_9=765+768=1533\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{for }r>1\text{ partial sums grow without bound, while for }|r|<1\text{ they approach a finite limit}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(S_8<1000\); (B) \(n=9\text{ already exceeds 1000; }S_\infty\text{ wrong}\); (C) \(S_9\text{ miscomputed as }3\cdot2^9\); \(S_\infty\text{ wrong}\).
Key point: \(S_n=a\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1};\ S_\infty=\dfrac a{1-r}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the member of a family of lines through the intersection of two lines that passes through the origin, and the image of a point in a line
questions.question: The lines \(2x+y-5=0\) and \(x-y-1=0\) meet at \(P\). Which line of the family \((2x+y-5)+\lambda(x-y-1)=0\) passes through the origin, and what is the image of \((1,2)\) in the line \(x+y-5=0\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(P=(2,1);\ x-2y=0;\ \text{image }(3,4)\)
Given: \(L_1:2x+y-5=0,\ L_2:x-y-1=0;\ \text{point }(1,2),\ \text{mirror }x+y-5=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(L_1+\lambda L_2=0\text{ passes through }L_1\cap L_2;\ \dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{-2(ax_1+by_1+c)}{a^2+b^2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{adding: }3x-6=0\Rightarrow x=2,\ y=1\)
Step 2: \((0,0):\ -5-\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-5\Rightarrow-3x+6y=0\Rightarrow x-2y=0\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{x-1}{1}=\dfrac{y-2}{1}=\dfrac{-2(1+2-5)}{2}=2\Rightarrow(3,4)\)
Worked derivation: \[(2x+y-5)-5(x-y-1)=-3x+6y=0\]
Check: \[\text{midpoint }(2,3)\text{ lies on }x+y=5;\ \text{segment direction }(2,2)\perp(1,-1)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{every member of the family vanishes at the common point, so one condition fixes }\lambda\text{; the image is symmetric about the mirror}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(P\text{ wrong}\); (C) \(\text{sign of }\lambda\text{ wrong; image through origin}\); (D) \(\text{gives the image in }y=x\).
Key point: \(L_1+\lambda L_2=0;\ \text{image formula with factor }-2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding conditions on k for x² + y² − 4x + 6y + k = 0 to be a real circle, to touch the x-axis or y-axis, and to be a point circle
questions.question: For \(x^2+y^2-4x+6y+k=0\), for which \(k\) is it a real circle, for which does it touch the \(x\)-axis, for which the \(y\)-axis, and for which is it a point circle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(k<13;\ k=4\ (x\text{-axis});\ k=9\ (y\text{-axis});\ k=13\ (\text{point circle})\)
Given: \(\text{centre }(2,-3),\ r^2=4+9-k=13-k\)
Formula/Principle: \(x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0:\ \text{centre }(-g,-f),\ r=\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}\)
Step 1: \(\text{real circle: }13-k>0\Rightarrow k<13;\ \text{point circle: }k=13\)
Step 2: \(\text{touches }x\text{-axis: }r=|{-3}|=3\Rightarrow13-k=9\Rightarrow k=4\)
Step 3: \(\text{touches }y\text{-axis: }r=|2|=2\Rightarrow13-k=4\Rightarrow k=9\)
Worked derivation: \[(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=13-k\]
Check: \[k=4:\ y=0\Rightarrow x^2-4x+4=0\Rightarrow(x-2)^2=0\ (\text{one point})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{tangency to an axis means the radius equals the centre's distance from that axis}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inequality reversed; axes swapped}\); (C) \(\text{axes swapped}\); (D) \(\text{signs wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{touches }x\text{-axis}\iff r=|f|;\ \text{touches }y\text{-axis}\iff r=|g|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the focus, directrix and latus rectum of a parabola, counting its lattice points in a range, and using the focal distance property
questions.question: For \(y^2=12x\), what are the focus, directrix and length of the latus rectum, how many points with integer coordinates and \(0\le x\le12\) lie on it, and what is the focal distance of \((3,6)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((3,0);\ x=-3;\ 12;\ 5\text{ points};\ 6\)
Given: \(y^2=12x=4ax\Rightarrow a=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{focus }(a,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-a,\ \text{latus rectum }4a;\ \text{focal distance}=x+a\)
Step 1: \(\text{focus }(3,0),\ \text{directrix }x=-3,\ \text{LR}=12\)
Step 2: \(x=\dfrac{y^2}{12}\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow6\mid y;\ y=0,\pm6,\pm12\Rightarrow x=0,3,12\Rightarrow5\text{ points}\)
Step 3: \(\text{focal distance of }(3,6)=3+3=6\)
Worked derivation: \[y^2=12x\text{ with }x\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow12\mid y^2\Rightarrow2\mid y,\ 3\mid y\Rightarrow6\mid y\]
Check: \[\sqrt{(3-3)^2+(6-0)^2}=6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a point on a parabola is as far from the focus as from the directrix}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{axis taken as vertical}\); (B) \(\text{directrix sign and LR wrong}\); (C) \(\text{uses }4a\text{ as }a\).
Key point: \(y^2=4ax:\ S(a,0),\ x=-a,\ \text{LR }4a,\ SP=x+a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating limits of rational functions by factorising and using the standard limit of (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a), including finding n from a given limit
questions.question: What are \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3-8}{x^2-4}\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x^2+2x}{5x^2-1}\), and for which positive integer \(n\) is \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^n-2^n}{x-2}=80\)?
options: A) \(\dfrac{12}{4}\text{ undefined};\ \dfrac25;\ 4\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(3;\ \dfrac35;\ n=5\)
Given: \(\text{three limits}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}=na^{n-1};\ \text{divide by the highest power for }x\to\infty\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{(x-2)(x^2+2x+4)}{(x-2)(x+2)}\to\dfrac{12}{4}=3\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{3+2/x}{5-1/x^2}\to\dfrac35\)
Step 3: \(n\cdot2^{n-1}=80\Rightarrow n=5\ (5\cdot16=80)\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3-2^3}{x^2-2^2}=\frac{3\cdot2^2}{2\cdot2}=3\]
Check: \[n=4:\ 4\cdot8=32;\ n=6:\ 6\cdot32=192\Rightarrow n=5\text{ unique}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the common factor }(x-a)\text{ removes the }0/0\text{ form, and at infinity only the leading terms matter}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the limit exists after cancelling}\); (C) \(\text{wrong cancellation and }n\); (D) \(\text{leading coefficients give }3/5\).
Key point: \(\lim\dfrac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}=na^{n-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an unknown number of balls in a bag from a given posterior probability using Bayes' theorem
questions.question: Bag I has \(4\) red and \(6\) black balls; bag II has \(k\) red and \(5\) black balls. A bag is chosen at random and a ball drawn from it is red. If the probability that it came from bag I is \(\tfrac13\), what is \(k\), and what is the probability that a randomly drawn ball is red?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(k=20;\ P(R)=0.60\)
Given: \(P(I)=P(II)=\tfrac12;\ P(R\mid I)=0.4;\ P(R\mid II)=\dfrac{k}{k+5};\ P(I\mid R)=\tfrac13\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(I\mid R)=\dfrac{P(I)P(R\mid I)}{P(I)P(R\mid I)+P(II)P(R\mid II)}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{0.4}{0.4+\frac{k}{k+5}}=\dfrac13\Rightarrow1.2=0.4+\dfrac{k}{k+5}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{k}{k+5}=0.8\Rightarrow k=0.8k+4\Rightarrow k=20\)
Step 3: \(P(R)=\tfrac12(0.4)+\tfrac12(0.8)=0.60\)
Worked derivation: \[P(I\mid R)=\frac{0.2}{0.2+0.4}=\frac13\]
Check: \[\text{bag II: }20\text{ red of }25=0.8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{Bayes' theorem links the posterior to the unknown likelihood, giving one equation in }k\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=10\text{ gives }P(I\mid R)=0.375\); (B) \(k=5\text{ gives }0.444\); (D) \(k=4\text{ gives }0.474\).
Key point: \(\text{posterior}=\dfrac{\text{prior}\times\text{likelihood}}{\text{total probability}}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving an inverse-tangent equation with the addition formula while checking principal values, and evaluating cos of a sum of inverse trigonometric values
questions.question: Solve \(\tan^{-1}(2x)+\tan^{-1}(3x)=\dfrac\pi4\), and find \(\cos\left(\sin^{-1}\tfrac35+\cos^{-1}\tfrac{12}{13}\right)\).
options: A) \(x=\tfrac16\text{ only};\ \tfrac{33}{65}\)
B) \(x=\tfrac16\text{ or }-1;\ \tfrac{33}{65}\)
C) \(x=-1\text{ only};\ \tfrac{63}{65}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x=\tfrac16;\ \tfrac{33}{65}\)
Given: \(\tan^{-1}2x+\tan^{-1}3x=\tfrac\pi4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{a+b}{1-ab}\ (ab<1);\ \cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{5x}{1-6x^2}=1\Rightarrow6x^2+5x-1=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac16\text{ or }-1\)
Step 2: \(x=-1:\ \tan^{-1}(-2)+\tan^{-1}(-3)<0\ne\tfrac\pi4\Rightarrow\text{reject};\ x=\tfrac16:\ ab=\tfrac16<1\ \checkmark\)
Step 3: \(\alpha=\sin^{-1}\tfrac35:\ \cos\alpha=\tfrac45;\ \beta=\cos^{-1}\tfrac{12}{13}:\ \sin\beta=\tfrac5{13}\Rightarrow\tfrac45\cdot\tfrac{12}{13}-\tfrac35\cdot\tfrac5{13}=\tfrac{33}{65}\)
Worked derivation: \[x=-1:\ \tan^{-1}(-2)+\tan^{-1}(-3)=-\pi+\tan^{-1}\frac{-5}{1-6}=-\frac{3\pi}{4}\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac16:\ \tan^{-1}\tfrac13+\tan^{-1}\tfrac12=\tan^{-1}\frac{5/6}{5/6}=\tfrac\pi4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the addition formula holds only when }ab<1\text{, so roots must be checked against the principal range}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=-1\text{ gives }-\tfrac{3\pi}4\); (C) \(\text{keeps only the extraneous root; uses }+\); (D) \(\text{wrong cosine value}\).
Key point: \(\text{check extraneous roots: the sum must lie in the required range}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing minors, cofactors and a 3 × 3 determinant by cofactor expansion, and the property that alien cofactors give zero
questions.question: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&4&5\\1&0&6\end{pmatrix}\), what are \(\det A\), the cofactors \(A_{12}\) and \(A_{21}\), and the value of \(a_{11}A_{21}+a_{12}A_{22}+a_{13}A_{23}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\det A=22;\ A_{12}=5,\ A_{21}=-12;\ 0\)
Given: \(A\text{ as above}\)
Formula/Principle: \(A_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij};\ \det A=\sum_j a_{1j}A_{1j};\ \sum_j a_{1j}A_{2j}=0\)
Step 1: \(\det A=1(24-0)-2(0-5)+3(0-4)=24+10-12=22\)
Step 2: \(A_{12}=-\begin{vmatrix}0&5\\1&6\end{vmatrix}=-(0-5)=5;\ A_{21}=-\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\0&6\end{vmatrix}=-12\)
Step 3: \(\text{row 1 elements with row 2 cofactors}=0\)
Worked derivation: \[A_{22}=\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\1&6\end{vmatrix}=3,\ A_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\1&0\end{vmatrix}=2;\ 1(-12)+2(3)+3(2)=0\]
Check: \[\text{expansion along column 1: }1(24)-0+1(10-12)=22\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{using another row's cofactors computes the determinant of a matrix with two equal rows, which is zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{signs of cofactors wrong}\); (C) \(\text{sign of }A_{12}\text{ wrong; alien sum is }0\); (D) \(\text{determinant and }A_{21}\text{ wrong}\).
Key point: \(\sum_j a_{ij}A_{kj}=\det A\text{ if }i=k,\ 0\text{ otherwise}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using logarithmic differentiation to find derivatives of xˣ and x^(1/x), locating their single critical points, and comparing 2^(1/2) with 3^(1/3)
questions.question: Using logarithmic differentiation, where does \(y=x^x\ (x>0)\) attain its minimum and what is the minimum value? Where does \(g(x)=x^{1/x}\ (x>0)\) attain its maximum, and which is larger, \(2^{1/2}\) or \(3^{1/3}\)?
options: D) \(x=\tfrac1e,\ \left(\tfrac1e\right)^{1/e};\ x=e;\ 3^{1/3}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\min\text{ at }x=\tfrac1e,\ \text{value }e^{-1/e};\ g\text{ max at }x=e;\ 3^{1/3}>2^{1/2}\)
Given: \(y=x^x,\ g=x^{1/x},\ x>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\ln y=x\ln x\Rightarrow\dfrac{y'}{y}=1+\ln x;\ \ln g=\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\Rightarrow\dfrac{g'}{g}=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}\)
Step 1: \(y'=x^x(1+\ln x)=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac1e;\ y'<0\text{ before},\ >0\text{ after}\Rightarrow\min=e^{-1/e}\)
Step 2: \(g'=x^{1/x}\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}=0\Rightarrow x=e;\ \text{sign }+\to-\Rightarrow\max\)
Step 3: \(3\text{ is closer to }e\text{ on the decreasing side}: 3^{1/3}\approx1.442>2^{1/2}\approx1.414\)
Worked derivation: \[\left(3^{1/3}\right)^6=9>8=\left(2^{1/2}\right)^6\Rightarrow3^{1/3}>2^{1/2}\]
Check: \[e^{-1/e}\approx0.692<1=1^1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{taking logs turns a variable exponent into a product that the product rule can handle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{points swapped}\); (B) \(y'(1)=1\ne0\); (C) \(\text{minimum value and comparison wrong}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}x^x=x^x(1+\ln x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Maximising the volume of an open box made by cutting equal squares from the corners of a square sheet, and the largest rectangle inscribed in a circle
questions.question: Equal squares of side \(x\) are cut from the corners of a square sheet of side \(18\text{ cm}\) and the sides folded up to make an open box. What \(x\) gives the largest volume and what is that volume? What is the largest area of a rectangle inscribed in a circle of radius \(r\)?
options: C) \(x=3;\ 432\text{ cm}^3;\ 2r^2\ (\text{a square})\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(x=3\text{ cm};\ V=432\text{ cm}^3;\ 2r^2\)
Given: \(V(x)=x(18-2x)^2,\ 0<x<9;\ \text{rectangle in circle radius }r\)
Formula/Principle: \(V'(x)=0,\ V''<0\Rightarrow\max\)
Step 1: \(V'=(18-2x)^2-4x(18-2x)=(18-2x)(18-6x)\)
Step 2: \(V'=0\Rightarrow x=3\ (x=9\text{ gives }V=0);\ V''(3)<0\)
Step 3: \(V(3)=3\cdot12^2=432;\ \text{rectangle }2r\cos\theta\times2r\sin\theta=2r^2\sin2\theta\le2r^2\)
Worked derivation: \[V''(x)=24x-144\Rightarrow V''(3)=-72<0\]
Check: \[V(2)=2\cdot196=392<432,\ V(4)=4\cdot100=400<432\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a deeper cut makes the box taller but its base smaller; the product peaks between the extremes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=9\text{ gives no box}\); (B) \(V(6)=216\text{ is not maximal; circle area is not a rectangle}\); (D) \(\text{volume and area wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{open box from side }a:\ x=a/6\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using integration by parts to find areas under y = ln x and y = x sin x
questions.question: What is the area of the region bounded by \(y=\ln x\), the \(x\)-axis and the line \(x=e\), and the area under \(y=x\sin x\) between \(x=0\) and \(x=\pi\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1;\ \pi\)
Given: \(y=\ln x\text{ on }[1,e];\ y=x\sin x\ge0\text{ on }[0,\pi]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du\)
Step 1: \(\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\ (u=\ln x,\ dv=dx)\)
Step 2: \([x\ln x-x]_1^e=(e-e)-(0-1)=1\)
Step 3: \(\int x\sin x\,dx=-x\cos x+\sin x\Rightarrow[-x\cos x+\sin x]_0^\pi=\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx=\left[-x\cos x\right]_0^\pi+\int_0^\pi\cos x\,dx=\pi+0\]
Check: \[\ln x\ge0\text{ on }[1,e]\text{ and area }1<1\cdot(e-1)\approx1.72\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{parts trades the awkward factor for its derivative, leaving an integral that is easy}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{evaluates }\ln\text{ wrongly; omits }x\); (C) \(\text{forgets the }-x\text{ term}\); (D) \(\text{doubles the second area}\).
Key point: \(\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating standard forms with quadratic denominators and square roots by completing the square, and studying the behaviour of the resulting function
